Resources
Resources
Laboratories: The department has all types of modern teaching- learning resources in the department.
The department is equipped with state-of-the-art laboratories, providing students with the necessary resources for practical learning and specialized software tools.
The technical staff is appointed by the institute and allotted by the Head of the department considering their skill set, by issuing formal order letters.
Adequate technical manpower ensures smooth laboratory operations, technical support, and assistance to students and faculty for academic and research activities. The list of laboratories and technical manpower is mentioned in Table
As and when any facility is created at the department in the form of hardware or software, the support staff is given training and certification to ensure their scaling up. Refer image below.
Data Structure & Programming Lab
A
Data Structures & Programming Lab
is a structured, practical companion to theory courses. Over 12–14 weeks, students can  implement core structures (arrays, lists, trees, graphs) in C/C++ (or Java/Python), Analyse algorithms, develop problem-solving skills, and learn memory management and file I/O.
The Programming Laboratory aims to provide students with hands-on experience in software development, problem-solving, and understanding computational logic. It equips learners with practical knowledge of programming languages, tools, and methodologies necessary for modern software development.
Resources: 1)Desktop 2) Projector 3) UPS
4)Windows + Ubuntu 5) Programming language
Knowledge Creation-
Collaborative problem-solving
: Students work in pairs/small groups on challenges like sorting algorithms, sharing approaches organically.
Practice
-driven mastery
: Lab assignments (e.g., implement BST or graph traversal repeatedly) convert explicit templates into tacit understanding.
Mini
-projects
: End-of-term projects embed multiple structures (lists + trees + hash maps), reinforcing application and internalization.
Innovation: Novel programming languages, paradigms, and tools.
Enhanced Productivity: Better compilers, IDEs, and debugging tools to streamline development.
Improved Education: Comprehensive learning resources for diverse audiences.
Industry Adoption: Real-world solutions for domains like healthcare, finance, etc.
Continuous
feedback
: Instructors highlight optimizations/improvements during labs to help students internalize best practices.
Free & Open Source Lab
Free & Open Source Lab,” releasing powerful tools and infrastructure openly. A Free & Open Source Lab refers to a research and development environment that emphasizes
open-source tools, collaboration, transparency
, and
accessibility.
This empower anyone to use, customize, and contribute to scientific or AI-driven software and hardware.
.
Resources: 1) Desktops 2) UPS 3) VScode 4) Ubuntu/Kali/CentOS
Knowledge creation in Free & Open Source (FOSS) labs is a richly collaborative, transparent, and continually evolving process.
It works as
Community-Led Knowledge Sharing & Co‑creation.
Computer Networking & Web Technology Lab
The
Computer Networking & Web Technology Lab
blends physical and virtual network experimentation with full-stack web application development. It equips students with practical and theoretical knowledge—from wiring NICs and routing protocols to building dynamic web services—ensuring hands-on competence in both networking and web technologies .
This lab empowers students to blend theory with hands-on practice by:
Building, configuring, and managing real and virtual
network devices
(NICs, routers, switches)
Setting up
network topologies
(LAN, WAN) and protocols across OSI/TCP‑IP layers
Implementing
Data Link and Network layer algorithms
(framing, error detection/correction, routing, congestion control)
Hosting
Web Technologies experiments
: HTML/CSS/JavaScript, PHP/MySQL,  XML, and server‑side scripting .
Resources:
1)Desktop 2) Projector 3) UPS
4) OS  5) NS2,NS3, Cisco packet tracer, Wire shark etc.
Microprocessor & IOT / Data Science Lab
A
Microprocessor & IoT Lab
is a specialized educational space designed to provide hands-on experience with microprocessors, microcontrollers, and Internet of Things (IoT) technologies. It serves as a practical environment where students can design, develop, and test embedded systems and IoT applications, bridging theoretical knowledge with real-world implementation.
The
Data Science Lab
is designed to provide students with hands-on experience in analysing and interpreting complex datasets. It serves as a bridge between theoretical knowledge and practical application, enabling students to:
·       Competence in presenting data insights through visualization
Resources:  1) Desktop 2) Projector 3) Printers 5) OS 6) Programing Language 7) IOT kits.8) GNU simulator, Sim 85, Proteus 9) VEKA, R language, Knime  etc.
Knowledge Creation-
Understand the microprocessor architecture, assembly language programming, and interfacing techniques.
Ability to design design and implement IOT system.
Enhance teamwork, communication, and project management skills in real world applications and Impact like smart home, healthcare ,industrial Automation ..
Understand the principles of data science and its real-world applications.
Develop proficiency in using data science tools and techniques.
Competence in presenting data insights through visualization.
Software Engineering Lab
Software Engineering Lab equips students with practical skills essential for a career in software development, fostering a deep understanding of the complexities involved in building and maintaining software systems.
Resources:   1) Desktop 2) Projector 3) Printers 5) OS 6) Programing Language
Knowledge Creation-
Collaborative Learning and Problem-Solving :
Students engage in group projects, such as developing software applications, where they collaboratively define problems, solutions, and implement code.
Industry-Academia Collaboration: By collaborating on real-world projects, students gain practical experience, and researchers receive valuable insights into industry challenges, leading to mutually beneficial knowledge exchange.
Software Engineering lab is a multifaceted process that combines individual learning with collaborative efforts. By leveraging tools, methodologies, and industry partnerships, this lab foster an environment where knowledge is continuously generated, shared, and refined. This dynamic process not only enhances students’ technical skills but also prepares them for the complexities of the software industry.
Project Lab
The Innovation and Project Laboratory is designed to foster creativity, problem-solving, and hands-on experience in building real-world projects. This lab aims to provide students with the tools, resources, and mentorship required to turn innovative ideas into functional prototypes or fully developed projects. The lab focuses on developing interdisciplinary skills, with a strong emphasis on collaborative project-based learning, research, and product development.
Resources:
1) Desktop 2) Smartboard 3)OS 4)MS office 5) Programming language etc.
Knowledge Creation-
Problem-Solving and Creativity: Ability to generate and implement innovative solutions for real-world problems.
Hands-on Experience: Gain practical experience in various interdisciplinary technologies, such as IoT, robotics, AI, and embedded systems.
Collaborative Skills: Develop teamwork, communication, and leadership skills through collaborative project work.
Entrepreneurial Skills: Understand the principles of turning ideas into marketable products and building a business around technology.
The Project Laboratory offers students an environment where they can take their ideas from concept to prototype, with access to cutting-edge tools, technology, and mentorship. This hands-on experience prepares them for careers in technology development, product design, entrepreneurship, and research.
PG Research Laboratory
The PG Research Laboratory is designed to support postgraduate students in conducting advanced research across various fields of technology, engineering, and applied sciences. The lab provides an environment conducive to deep academic exploration, allowing students to engage in both theoretical research and practical experiments. The goal is to foster innovative research, develop new technologies, and contribute to scientific advancements.
Resources: 1) Desktop 2) Smartboard 3)OS 4)MS office 5) Programming language etc.
Knowledge Creation-
Research Competence: Gain proficiency in conducting high-quality research in various domains of technology and engineering.
Problem-Solving Skills: Develop advanced problem-solving skills to tackle real-world challenges through innovative solutions.
Advanced Technical Knowledge: Deepen expertise in specific research areas such as AI, IoT,Data science.
Academic Publishing: Ability to write and publish research papers in reputable conferences and journals.
Collaboration: Work collaboratively in research teams, both within the lab and with external stakeholders.
The PG Research Laboratory provides an ideal environment for postgraduate students to deepen their expertise, engage in cutting-edge research, and contribute to advancements in science and technology. It equips students with the tools and experience necessary to pursue successful careers in research, academia, or industry.

Mission
To achieve above Vision, all stakeholders of this programme are committed to following missions-
M1
: Adopting vibrant curricula and teaching practices to  equip graduates with strong foundations in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning.
M2
: Providing opportunities to develop professional skills through academic excellence, industry exposure and interdisciplinary collaborations.
M3
: Empowering students with critical thinking and problem-solving skills to develop innovative solutions.
M4
: Inculcating lifelong learning and ethical responsibility towards society and the environment
Strength
The Department of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning stands out for its key strengths, which include:
Industry-Aligned Curriculum
Experienced and Research-Oriented Faculty
Advanced Laboratory Infrastructure
Strong Research and Innovation Culture
Emphasis on Experiential Learning
Robust Industry Collaboration
Focus on Ethical and Responsible AI
Holistic Student Development
Global Exposure Opportunities
Supportive Alumni Network
These strengths collectively position the department as a leader in AIML education, research, and innovation.
Areas of Expertise
The Department of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning excels in the following areas of expertise:
Artificial Intelligence & Intelligent Systems
Machine Learning & Deep Learning
Natural Language Processing (NLP)
Computer Vision & Image Processing
Data Science & Big Data Analytics
Cybersecurity & AI for Security
Edge AI & Embedded Intelligence
Computer Networks and Distributed Systems
Cloud Computing & AI Deployment
Blockchain and Decentralized Applications
Open-Source Development and Contributions
High Performance Computing
These areas of expertise enable the department to provide students with advanced knowledge and practical skills, preparing them for leadership roles in the ever-evolving technology landscape.
Silent Department Features
The Department of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning at Walchand College of Engineering stands out for its unique features and strengths, including:
Academic Excellence:
Industry-aligned curriculum focusing on foundational and advanced topics.
Highly qualified faculty with expertise in cutting-edge technologies. Nearly 90% of faculties are PhD registered.
State-of-the-Art Infrastructure:
Modern computer labs are equipped with high-performance systems.
Access to advanced tools, software, and cloud computing platforms.
Research and Innovation:
Active research in emerging fields like AI, machine learning, data science, and IoT.
Regular publications in reputed journals and conference participations with scopus and SCI indexing.
Strong Industry Interface:
Collaborations with leading tech companies for internships, placements, and projects.
Industry-expert guest lectures, workshops, and certifications.
Skill Development Opportunities:
Emphasis on hands-on learning through hackathons, coding challenges, and projects.
Active technical clubs and student organizations fostering innovation.
Global Competence:
Alumni placed in top organizations and pursuing higher education globally.
Exposure to international competitions and exchange programs.
Student-Centric Environment:
Personalized mentoring by faculty for academic and professional growth.
Focus on holistic development through extracurricular and co-curricular activities.
Placement Excellence:
High placement rates with opportunities in top companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft.
Dedicated training for technical interviews, coding tests, and soft skills.
Continuous Improvement:
Regular updates to the curriculum and teaching methodologies.
Feedback-driven enhancements for a superior learning experience.
These features collectively position the department as a leader in producing highly skilled, innovative, and socially responsible engineers.
Leadership
Dr. Rathod Ravindra Ramkishan
(Head of the Department of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning)
Dr. RATHOD RAVINDRA RAMKISHAN is the Head of the Department of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning at Walchand College of Engineering, Sangli. He joined the institution in 2004 and has since made significant contributions to the field of IT,  computer science, Artificial Intelligence education and research. Dr. Rathod holds a Ph.D. in Computer Science and Engineering from Indian Institute of Technology Roorkee.. he also earned his M.E.. degrees in Computer Science and Engineering from Walchand College of Engineering and B.E MGM’s College of Engineering, Nanded. Swami Ramanand Teerth Marathwada University, Nanded.
His research interests include Data Mining, GIS, AI, Image Processing and Applications. Dr. Rathod has published numerous papers in national and international journals and conferences. He has also been involved in several sponsored projects. Dr. R.R. Rathod’s published patent stands as a testament to his contribution toward technological innovation and the promotion of research-driven academic excellence.
He has been awarded with Padmashree S.M.Annasaheb Behare “Ideal Teacher Commendable Prize-2009” at Walchand College of Engineering, Sangli.

In 2024, D. B. Kulkarni co-authored several notable publications. These include

, and

.
B. Kulkarni also contributed to

alongside R. Sharma, R. Anuradha, V. Sathian, and P. Choudhury, and
“Standardization of 109Cd Using CIEMAT/NIST Method and Internal Conversion Electron Counting”
with the same team, both published in

. His work on

appeared in

.
B. Kulkarni contributed to

and
“National Audit for Traceable 131I Activity Measurements with Radionuclide Calibrators Among Nuclear Medicine Centers in India”
, both in

.
In 2023, D. B. Kulkarni co-authored

with S. Sayyad in

, and also contributed to
“Development of FPGA-based Standalone, Portable TDCR System”
in

.

with A. Shikalgar, which was published in the
Journal of Ambient Intelligence and Humanized Computing
, Volume 15, Issue 8, pages 3255–3272.
In 2024 Dr. Sonavane collaborated with M. S. Dabade, G. R. Shinde, and A. M. Chimanna on the paper
“Automatic Bone Cancer Detection – A Comprehensive Survey”
, published in
Grenze International Journal of Engineering & Technology (GIJET)
, Volume 10, Issue 1.
In 2023, Dr. Sonavane co-authored
“SARP: Secure Routing Protocol Using Anonymous Authentication in Vehicular Ad-hoc Networks”
with B. Yelure, published in the
Journal of Ambient Intelligence and Humanized Computing
, Volume 14, Issue 4, pages 3567–3581.
In 2023, Dr. Sonavane collaborated with S. B. Nemade on the work
“Semantic Segmentation Using GSAUNet”
, which appeared in
ICT Express
, Volume 9, Issue 1, pages 1–7.

, along with N. Gavankar, V. Waghmare, and M. Bokare. This paper was presented at the
2nd DMIHER International Conference on Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare
.
Rathod also collaborated with N. Gavankar and V. Waghmare on the paper
“Estimation of Height of Building Using High Resolution Satellite Image”
, presented at the
International Conference on Geographical Information Systems Theory
.
In 2023, Dr. Rathod contributed to multiple research articles published in the
Indian Journal of Technical Education (IJTE)
. One of the papers,
“Gesture Recognition for Deaf and Dumb People”
, co-authored with S. Bhowate, S. Ruikar, and A. Umbarkar, appeared in the special issue on pages 308–314. Another paper titled
“AHP Based Techno-Economic Analysis of Energy Management of Radial Distribution Network using Optimal DG and Capacitor Placements and Sizing”
, co-authored with S. S. Tanwar, G. P. Prajapat, and S. Sisodiya, was published in the same special issue on pages 82–90.
Rathod also contributed to the work
“Hybrid VARMA-LSTM Approach for Forecasting Wind Power Density in Jaipur, Rajasthan”
, in collaboration with S. Yadav, H. Kumar, and S. S. Tanwar, which was published in the same journal (pages 31–36). Additionally, the paper
“Intelligent Artificial Control and Multilayer Inverter Based Improved Control of a Wind Power System based DFIG”
, co-authored with S. S. Tanwar, G. P. Prajapat, and D. D. Kshirsagar, was included in the special issue on pages 37–43.

in

B.Tech Curriculum with Minors
B.Tech Curriculum with Minors
Curriculum
– The B. Tech curriculum in Robotics and Automation is designed to provide students with a comprehensive education in Robotics and Automation engineering.
Curriculum
– The B. Tech curriculum in Robotics and Automation engineering is designed to provide students with a comprehensive education in Robotics and Automation engineering. In the Academic Year 2025-2026 curriculum of Second Year is implemented as per NEP 2020 policy which includes multidisciplinary minor (MDM) as well. Robotics and Automation engineering department offers MDM in Robotic Fundamentals and Design.
Knowledge and Attitude Profile (WK)
WK1:
A systematic, theory-based understanding of the natural sciences applicable to the discipline and awareness of relevant social sciences.
WK2:
Conceptually-based mathematics, numerical analysis, data analysis, statistics and formal aspects of computer and information science to support detailed analysis and modelling applicable to the discipline.
WK3:
A systematic, theory-based formulation of engineering fundamentals required in the engineering discipline.
WK4:
Engineering specialist knowledge that provides theoretical frameworks and bodies of knowledge for the accepted practice areas in the engineering discipline; much is at the forefront of the discipline.
WK5:
Knowledge, including efficient resource use, environmental impacts, whole-life cost, reuse of resources, net zero carbon, and similar concepts, that supports engineering design and operations in a practice area.
WK6:
Knowledge of engineering practice (technology) in the practice areas in the engineering discipline.
WK7:
Knowledge of the role of engineering in society and identified issues in engineering practice in the discipline, such as the professional responsibility of an engineer to public safety and sustainable development.
WK8:
Engagement with selected knowledge in the current research literature of the discipline, awareness of the power of critical thinking and creative approaches to evaluate emerging issues.
WK9:
Ethics, inclusive behavior and conduct. Knowledge of professional ethics, responsibilities, and norms of engineering practice. Awareness of the need for diversity by reason of ethnicity, gender, age, physical ability etc. with mutual understanding and respect, and of inclusive attitudes
Program Objective and Outcome
Graduates of UG Programme after completing their graduation in Robotics and Automation Engineering will be able to:
PEO1:
Demonstrate technical competency by applying knowledge to solve problems related to Engineering issues.
PEO2:
Exhibit high professional skills and ethical attitude to succeed in their professional career.
PEO3:
Display thirst for emerging technologies and quest for research and innovation to solve real-world problems of high complexity, with concern to society and environment
Program outcomes
PO1: Engineering Knowledge:
Apply knowledge of mathematics, natural science, computing, engineering fundamentals and an engineering specialization as specified in WK1 to WK4 respectively to develop to the solution of complex engineering problems.
PO2: Problem Analysis:
Identify, formulate, review research literature and analyze complex engineering problems reaching substantiated conclusions with consideration for sustainable development. (WK1 to WK4)
PO3:
Design/Development of Solutions:
Design creative solutions for complex engineering problems and design/develop systems/components/processes to meet identified needs with consideration for the public health and safety, whole-life cost, net zero carbon, culture, society and environment as required. (WK5)
PO4:
Conduct Investigations of Complex Problems:
Conduct investigations of complex engineering problems using research-based knowledge including design of experiments, modelling, analysis & interpretation of data to provide valid conclusions. (WK8).
PO5:
Engineering Tool Usage:
Create, select and apply appropriate techniques, resources and modern engineering & IT tools, including prediction and modelling recognizing their limitations to solve complex engineering problems. (WK2 and WK6)
PO6:
The Engineer and The World:
Analyze and evaluate societal and environmental aspects while solving complex engineering problems for its impact on sustainability with reference to economy, health, safety, legal framework, culture and environment. (WK1, WK5, and WK7).
PO7:
Ethics:
Apply ethical principles and commit to professional ethics, human values, diversity and inclusion; adhere to national & international laws. (WK9)
PO8:
Individual and Collaborative Team work:
Function effectively as an individual, and as a member or leader in diverse/multi-disciplinary teams.
PO9:
Communication:
Communicate effectively and inclusively within the engineering community and society at large, such as being able to comprehend and write effective reports and design documentation, make effective presentations considering cultural, language, and learning differences
PO10:
Project Management and Finance:
Apply knowledge and understanding of engineering management principles and economic decision-making and apply these to multidisciplinary environments.
PO11:
Life-Long Learning:
Recognize the need for, and have the preparation and ability for i) independent and life-long learning ii) adaptability to new and emerging technologies and iii) critical thinking in the broadest context of technological change. (WK8)
Program Specific Outcomes
PSO1:
Gain the necessary knowledge, ability to design and implement innovative and state-of-the-art solutions for complex problems in automation, robotics and cross disciplinary domains.
PSO2:
Integration and applications of automation and robotics to identify the needs, design, select and integrate appropriate automation and robotic subsystems for diverse applications.
Outcome based Educational Philosophy
Outcome-Based Education (OBE) focuses on achieving specific outcomes in terms of knowledge, skills, and attitudes that students are expected to demonstrate upon graduation. For a B.Tech in Robotics and Automation Engineering (RA), the OBE philosophy aligns with the program’s mission to develop competent engineers capable of solving real-world problems using modern computing technologies.
Focus on Graduate Attributes
:
OBE emphasizes the development of key attributes such as problem-solving, critical thinking, teamwork, and effective communication, which are essential for robotics engineers.
Student- Centred Learning
:
The learning process is tailored to meet the needs and aspirations of the students, ensuring that each learner achieves predefined outcomes.
Clear Definition of Learning Outcomes
:
Learning outcomes are categorized into
Program Outcomes (POs)
,
Program Specific Outcomes (PSOs)
, and
Course Outcomes (COs)
:
POs
: Define general competencies (e.g., problem analysis, ethical responsibility).
PSOs
: Focus on domain-specific skills (e.g., software development, AI applications).
COs
: Specify what students will achieve in individual courses.
Alignment Across Levels
:
The curriculum, teaching methodologies, and assessment strategies are aligned with achieving the defined outcomes.
Continuous Assessment and Feedback
:
The OBE framework uses tools like rubrics, surveys, and assessments to measure outcomes and provide feedback for continuous improvement.
Preparation for Lifelong Learning
:
Encourages adaptability and lifelong learning to remain relevant in a rapidly evolving field like Robotics and Automation Engineering.

B.Tech Curriculum with Minors
B.Tech Curriculum with Minors
Curriculum
– The B.Tech curriculum in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning is designed to provide students with a comprehensive education in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning.
Curriculum
– The B.Tech curriculum in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning is designed to provide students with a comprehensive education in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning. In the Academic Year 2024-2025 curriculum of First year and Academic Year 2025-2026 Second Year is implemented as per NEP 2020 policy which includes multidisciplinary minor (MDM) as well. AIML department offers MDM in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (14 credits).
Minors –
The department offers minors in areas such as artificial intelligence, Machine Learning,
Program Objective and Outcome
Under-Graduate PEOs –
PEO1:
Demonstrate Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning knowledge to design an engineering solution.
PEO2:
Exhibit communicative and professional skills with ethical human values for the use of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning.
PEO3:
Develop an aptitude for reflective and continuous learning with emerging trends and technologies of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning.
Program Outcomes
PO1: Engineering Knowledge:
Apply knowledge of mathematics, natural science, computing, engineering fundamentals and an engineering specialization as specified in WK1 to WK4 respectively to develop to the solution of complex engineering problems.
PO2: Problem Analysis:
Identify, formulate, review research literature and analyze complex engineering problems reaching substantiated conclusions with consideration for sustainable development. (WK1 to WK4)
PO3: Design/Development of Solutions:
Design creative solutions for complex engineering problems and design/develop systems/components/processes to meet identified needs with consideration for the public health and safety, whole-life cost, net zero carbon, culture, society and environment as required. (WK5)
PO4: Conduct Investigations of Complex Problems:
Conduct investigations of complex engineering problems using research-based knowledge including design of experiments, modeling, analysis & interpretation of data to provide valid conclusions. (WK8).
PO5: Engineering Tool Usage:
Create, select and apply appropriate techniques, resources and modern engineering & IT tools, including prediction and modeling recognizing their limitations to solve complex engineering problems. (WK2 and WK6)
PO6: The Engineer and The World:
Analyze and evaluate societal and environmental aspects while solving complex engineering problems for its impact on sustainability with reference to economy, health, safety, legal framework, culture and environment. (WK1, WK5, and WK7).
PO7: Ethics:
Apply ethical principles and commit to professional ethics, human values, diversity and inclusion; adhere to national & international laws. (WK9)
PO8: Individual and Collaborative Team work:
Function effectively as an individual, and as a member or leader in diverse/multi-disciplinary teams.
PO9: Communication:
Communicate effectively and inclusively within the engineering community and society at large, such as being able to comprehend and write effective reports and design documentation, make effective presentations considering cultural, language, and learning differences
PO10: Project Management and Finance:
Apply knowledge and understanding of engineering management principles and economic decision-making and apply these to one’s own work, as a member and leader in a team, and to manage projects and in multidisciplinary environments.
PO11: Life-Long Learning:
Recognize the need for, and have the preparation and ability for
i) Independent and life-long learning
ii) adaptability to new and emerging technologies
iii) critical thinking in the broadest context of technological change. (WK8)
Program Specific Outcomes
Under-Graduate PSOs –
PSO1:
Apply knowledge to synthesis, analyze and design algorithmic solutions in project  development process
PSO2:
Conceptualize knowledge to use advance AI ML techniques to analyze and design  algorithms, solve problems
Outcome Based Educational Philosophy
The Department of Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning adopts an
Outcome-Based Education (OBE)
philosophy that emphasizes achieving clearly defined learning outcomes and continuous improvement in the teaching-learning process. This approach ensures that students not only acquire theoretical knowledge but also demonstrate measurable competencies aligned with industry, academia, and societal expectations.
Learner-Centric Approach:
Focus on what students are expected to learn and demonstrate, shifting from traditional teaching to outcome-driven learning.
Clearly Defined Outcomes:
Formulation of Program Educational Objectives (PEOs), Program Outcomes (POs), and Course Outcomes (COs) aligned with Bloom’s taxonomy and Washington Accord guidelines.
Curriculum Alignment and Mapping:
All curriculum components are mapped to defined outcomes through curriculum matrix and assessment rubrics.
Continuous Assessment and Feedback:
Use of formative and summative assessments (quizzes, assignments, projects, etc.) to evaluate the attainment of outcomes and improve instructional strategies.
Graduate Attributes Integration:
Emphasis on critical thinking, ethical reasoning, teamwork, communication, lifelong learning, and professional responsibility.
Data-Driven Improvement:
Regular analysis of CO-PO attainment data to identify gaps, redesign course delivery, and improve academic performance.
Industry and Societal Relevance:
Curriculum and outcomes are constantly revised based on feedback from industry experts, alumni, employers, and academic peers to ensure relevance and employability.

Resources
Resources
The Department of Humanities and Sciences at Walchand College of Engineering (WCE), Sangli, is equipped with modern teaching-learning resources to support foundational education and holistic development of engineering students. The department houses state-of-the-art laboratories, advanced software tools, and skilled technical staff to facilitate practical learning, research, and skill development. Below is an overview of the key laboratory resources and associated technical manpower.
Laboratories:
The department maintains well-equipped laboratories designed to provide hands-on experience and foster interdisciplinary learning in sciences and humanities. These laboratories are supported by modern infrastructure, specialized equipment, and trained technical staff to ensure seamless operations and effective learning outcomes.
Engineering Chemistry Laboratory
Purpose
:
Provides practical training in chemical analysis, material properties, and environmental chemistry, aligning with the engineering curriculum.
Facilities
:
Advanced analytical instruments such as pH meters, conductivity meters, and UV-Vis spectrophotometers.
Equipment for experiments on corrosion, water analysis, and polymer synthesis.
Safety equipment including fume hoods, fire extinguishers, and chemical storage cabinets.
Engineering Physics Laboratory
Purpose
:
Facilitates experiments in mechanics, optics, electricity, and modern physics to strengthen students’ understanding of physical principles.
Facilities
:
Optical benches for experiments in diffraction, interference, and polarization.
Equipment for studying semiconductor properties, Hall effect, and quantum mechanics.
High-precision instruments like laser sources, oscilloscopes, and function generators.
Language Laboratory
Purpose
:
Enhances communication skills, technical writing, and professional presentation abilities through interactive language learning.
Facilities
:
Computer workstations with language learning software Orell Talk.
Audio-visual systems for pronunciation practice, listening exercises, and group discussions.
High-speed internet for accessing online language resources and e-learning platforms.
Software Tools: Language learning applications and tools for grammar, vocabulary, and public speaking.
Applications: Supports English language courses and prepares students for global communication and placement interviews.
Virtual Laboratory for German Language
Purpose
:
Provides an immersive learning environment for all as it is open to all by one click and to acquire proficiency in German, supporting the department’s foreign language offerings.
Facilities
:
Cloud-based virtual lab with interactive modules for German grammar, vocabulary, and conversational practice.

Students Development
Students Development
Student Development Activities (Academic Year 2024–25)
The Department of Humanities and Sciences at Walchand College of Engineering, Sangli, is committed to fostering holistic development among First Year B.Tech students. During the academic year 2024–25, the department conducted several activities and initiatives that supported students’ academic, emotional, social, and professional growth.
1. Voter Card Registration Drive
As a part of civic awareness and responsibility, the department organized a
Voter Card Registration Drive
for first-year students. In conjunction with this,
an Essay Writing Competition
and
Wallpaper Presentation Competition
were held to encourage students to reflect on the significance of democratic participation. Topics revolved around the importance of voting, youth empowerment, and democratic values.
2. Attendance of First year students to Sakal Series: Expert Lectures Series
In collaboration with the
Sakal Media Group
, a series of expert lectures was arranged on the topics of
Artificial Intelligence
,
Career Opportunities in New Technologies
, and
Industry 4.0
. Eminent speakers from academia and industry guided students about skill demands, future job trends, and career planning.
3. Mentor-Mentee Scheme
The department successfully implemented the
Mentor-Mentee Scheme
exclusively for first-year students. Unlike the second-year model aligned with NEP, the first-year initiative had distinct objectives:
Addressing the individual needs and backgrounds of students.
Focusing on transition from school to professional education.
Building confidence and offering emotional support.
Each mentor was assigned a group of 20-23 mentees. Regular meetings were held to ensure continuous interaction and academic/personal support.
4. Query Resolution Session
To ensure timely academic support and clarification,
daily Query Resolution Sessions
were organized between
5:30 PM and 6:00 PM
in Physics and Chemistry Labs. Subject faculty and coordinators addressed students’ doubts related to academics, exams, and language skills. This initiative greatly benefited slow and average learners.
5. World Environment Day Celebration
On the occasion of
World Environment Day (June 5, 2024)
, the department initiated a campaign titled
“Say No to Plastic”
. Activities included:
Students taking a pledge to reduce plastic use.
Awareness rallies and poster-making competitions.
A proposal was submitted to the administration to reduce plastic use on campus.
6. Jayanti Celebrations
To instil values and inspire students, the department celebrated
birth/death anniversaries (Jayantis)
of great personalities such as:
A.P.J. Abdul Kalam
Swami Vivekananda
Savitribai Phule
Students presented speeches, essays, and short skits portraying the lives and teachings of these figures. The objective was to connect students with India’s rich legacy of leadership and service.
7. Induction Programme
The department participated in a
five-day Induction Programme
at the beginning of the academic year, consisting of:
Expert lectures on emotional intelligence, career building, and engineering ethics.
Yoga and meditation sessions.
Campus familiarization tours.
Ice-breaking games and team-building activities.
This helped in smooth academic transition and integration of students into the campus environment.
8. Internship Programmes
First-year students were encouraged to participate in internships through the
MyPerfectice Platform
. The Department of Humanities and Sciences actively monitored their registrations and progress on the platform. Counselling support was provided to students facing technical or registration issues. Many students availed
free-of-cost online internship modules
in areas like soft skills, design thinking, and emerging technologies.
9. Skill Development Programme
Proposals for skill development workshops were initiated focusing on:
English Communication Skills
Presentation Techniques
Public Speaking and Personality Development
Email Writing and Business Communication
These modules are designed to enhance employability and confidence among students, and sessions will be conducted in collaboration with the Training and Placement Cell.
10. Guidance to Higher-Class Students in Projects and Patent Work
The Department of Humanities and Sciences actively supports not only first-year students but also extends academic and research mentorship to senior and postgraduate students. As a significant contribution,
Dr. R. P. Gurav
from the department has been guiding
Mr. Niranjan Nitin Patil
, an M.Tech student, in developing an innovative project titled
“Water-Based Intumescent Paint”
.
The successful submission of the
patent application and copyright claim
for this project reflects the department’s commitment to fostering a culture of research, innovation, and intellectual property awareness among students. Such initiatives serve as inspirational examples for first-year learners and encourage interdisciplinary collaboration and innovation across batches.

B Tech Curriculum with Minors
B Tech Curriculum with Minors
The B. Tech curriculum in MDM Centre is designed to provide students with a comprehensive education in respective MDM stream.
In the Academic Year 2025-2026 curriculum of Third Year is implemented as per NEP 2020 policy which includes multidisciplinary minor (MDM) as well.
Knowledge and Attitude Profile (WK)
WK1:
A systematic, theory-based understanding of the natural sciences applicable to the discipline and awareness of relevant social sciences.
WK2:
Conceptually-based mathematics, numerical analysis, data analysis, statistics and formal aspects of computer and information science to support detailed analysis and modelling applicable to the discipline.
WK3:
A systematic, theory-based formulation of engineering fundamentals required in the engineering discipline.
WK4:
Engineering specialist knowledge that provides theoretical frameworks and bodies of knowledge for the accepted practice areas in the engineering discipline; much is at the forefront of the discipline.
WK5:
Knowledge, including efficient resource use, environmental impacts, whole-life cost, reuse of resources, net zero carbon, and similar concepts, that supports engineering design and operations in a practice area.
WK6:
Knowledge of engineering practice (technology) in the practice areas in the engineering discipline.
WK7:
Knowledge of the role of engineering in society and identified issues in engineering practice in the discipline, such as the professional responsibility of an engineer to public safety and sustainable development.
WK8:
Engagement with selected knowledge in the current research literature of the discipline, awareness of the power of critical thinking and creative approaches to evaluate emerging issues.
WK9:
Ethics, inclusive behavior and conduct. Knowledge of professional ethics, responsibilities, and norms of engineering practice. Awareness of the need for diversity by reason of ethnicity, gender, age, physical ability etc. with mutual understanding and respect, and of inclusive attitudes.
Objectives & Outcomes
Program objectives:
Graduates of UG Programme after completing their graduation in the Engineering with respective Minor stream they will be able to:
PEO1:
Demonstrate technical competency by applying knowledge to solve problems related to Engineering issues.
PEO2:
Exhibit high professional skills and ethical attitude to succeed in their professional career.
PEO3:
Display thirst for emerging technologies and quest for research and innovation to solve real-world problems of high complexity, with concern to society and environment.
Program outcomes:
PO1: Engineering Knowledge:
Apply knowledge of mathematics, natural science, computing, engineering fundamentals and an engineering specialization as specified in WK1 to WK4 respectively to develop to the solution of complex engineering problems.
PO2: Problem Analysis:
Identify, formulate, review research literature and analyze complex engineering problems reaching substantiated conclusions with consideration for sustainable development. (WK1 to WK4)
PO3:
Design/Development of Solutions:
Design creative solutions for complex engineering problems and design/develop systems/components/processes to meet identified needs with consideration for the public health and safety, whole-life cost, net zero carbon, culture, society and environment as required. (WK5)
PO4:
Conduct Investigations of Complex Problems:
Conduct investigations of complex engineering problems using research-based knowledge including design of experiments, modelling, analysis & interpretation of data to provide valid conclusions. (WK8).
PO5:
Engineering Tool Usage:
Create, select and apply appropriate techniques, resources and modern engineering & IT tools, including prediction and modelling recognizing their limitations to solve complex engineering problems. (WK2 and WK6)
PO6:
The Engineer and The World:
Analyze and evaluate societal and environmental aspects while solving complex engineering problems for its impact on sustainability with reference to economy, health, safety, legal framework, culture and environment. (WK1, WK5, and WK7).
PO7:
Ethics:
Apply ethical principles and commit to professional ethics, human values, diversity and inclusion; adhere to national & international laws. (WK9)
PO8:
Individual and Collaborative Team work:
Function effectively as an individual, and as a member or leader in diverse/multi-disciplinary teams.
PO9:
Communication:
Communicate effectively and inclusively within the engineering community and society at large, such as being able to comprehend and write effective reports and design documentation, make effective presentations considering cultural, language, and learning differences
PO10:
Project Management and Finance:
Apply knowledge and understanding of engineering management principles and economic decision-making and apply these to multidisciplinary environments.
PO11:
Life-Long Learning:
Recognize the need for, and have the preparation and ability for i) independent and life-long learning ii) adaptability to new and emerging technologies and iii) critical thinking in the broadest context of technological change. (WK8)
Program specific outcomes:
PSO1:
Gain the necessary knowledge, ability to design and implement innovative and state-of-the-art solutions for complex problems in respective MDM stream.
PSO2:
Integration and applications of to identify the needs, design, select and integrate appropriate solution for diverse applications.
Outcome based Educational Philosophy –
Outcome-Based Education (OBE) focuses on achieving specific outcomes in terms of knowledge, skills, and attitudes that students are expected to demonstrate upon graduation. For a B.Tech, the OBE philosophy aligns with the program’s mission to develop competent engineers capable of solving real-world problems using modern computing technologies.
Focus on Graduate Attributes
:
OBE emphasizes the development of key attributes such as problem-solving, critical thinking, teamwork, and effective communication, which are essential for robotics engineers.
Student- Centred Learning
:
The learning process is tailored to meet the needs and aspirations of the students, ensuring that each learner achieves predefined outcomes.
Clear Definition of Learning Outcomes
:
Learning outcomes are categorized into
Program Outcomes (POs)
,
Program Specific Outcomes (PSOs)
, and
Course Outcomes (COs)
:
POs
: Define general competencies (e.g., problem analysis, ethical responsibility).
PSOs
: Focus on domain-specific skills (e.g., software development, AI applications).
COs
: Specify what students will achieve in individual courses.
Alignment Across Levels
:
The curriculum, teaching methodologies, and assessment strategies are aligned with achieving the defined outcomes.
Continuous Assessment and Feedback
:
The OBE framework uses tools like rubrics, surveys, and assessments to measure outcomes and provide feedback for continuous improvement.
Preparation for Lifelong Learning
:
Encourages adaptability and lifelong learning to remain relevant in a rapidly evolving field of respective MDM stream.

Course Objectives
This is the first course in the Geotechnical Engineering domain. It is designed to let students understand the
mechanical behavior of soil/Earthen materials under stresses specifically when they interact with Civil
Engineering structures. It is also intended to cover the requisite contents of important competitive
examinations and entrance examinations for higher studies.
Course Outcomes (CO)
Blooms Taxonomy
CO Description
Descriptor Level
Explain soil properties, laboratory determination, soil classification,
CO1 Understanding II
and behavior of soils affecting Civil Engineering structures.
CO2 Determine effective stresses in soil under static and seepage conditions. Applying III
CO3 Estimate the soil settlement and time required under a given load Evaluating V
CO4 Determine soil strength & deformation parameters from soil tests Applying III
Module Module Contents Hours
Introduction: Description of soil, review of engineering geology, clay mineralogy,
I Scope of Geotechnical Engineering, Three-phase system and phase relationships, 6
Determination of various Index Properties of Soil in the laboratory
Soil Classification: Grain size and hydrometer analysis, Plasticity Characteristics of
II 5
Soil and their determination, Unified and IS soil classification system
Permeability and Seepage: Soil-water Statics, Principle of effective stress, One-
dimensional flow, Darcy’s law, laboratory methods for determination of coefficient of
III 8
permeability. Seepage through soils - two-dimensional flow, flow nets, uplift pressure,
piping, criteria for filter design; quicksand condition, liquefaction, mud-pumping
Compaction of Soils: Definition and importance of compaction, Comparison between
compaction and consolidation, Effect of compaction on soil properties, Theory of
IV 5
compaction, Laboratory determination of optimum moisture content and maximum dry
density, Compaction in the field: specifications and quality control.
Compressibility of Soils: Initial, primary & secondary consolidation, spring analogy,
Terzaghi’s theory of consolidation, Procedure and Interpretation of consolidation test
V results, 2:1 approximate method and Bouusinesq’s theory to determine vertical stress 9

Course Objectives
To introduce the various mechanisms of heat and mass transfer that characterizes a given physical
1
system.
2 To make the students familiarize conservation equations along with models for heat transfer processes.
To prepare the students for analysis of one-dimensional steady and unsteady partial differential
3
equations.
4 To train the students to develop representative models of real-life heat transfer processes and systems
Course Outcomes (CO) with Bloom’s Taxonomy Level
At the end of the course, the students will be able to,
Bloom’s Bloom’s
CO Course Outcome Statement/s Taxonomy Taxonomy
Level Description
CO1 Demonstrate the basic laws of heat and mass transfer and compute heat
III Applying
transfer rates.
CO2 Analyze problems involving steady and transient state heat transfer. IV Analysing

CO3 Assess the performance of thermal systems under different operating and V Evaluating
geometrical conditions.
CO4 Design the two fluid Heat Exchangers for different applications V Evaluating
Module Module Contents Hours
Introduction
Introduction to Heat transfer, difference between thermodynamics and heat transfer,
I 4
modes of heat transfer. laws of heat transfer, thermal conductivity coefficient of heat
transfer and Boiling & Condensation ( Theory part)
Conduction
Simple steady state problems in heat conduction, concept of thermal resistance and
conductance. General equation of temperature field in three dimensional Cartesian
coordinate systems. Application of above (one dimensional case) equation to the
system of plane wall (including composite structure) as well as to the system with
II radial heat conduction i.e. cylinders and Sphere (including composite structures). 9
Steady state conduction one dimensional) through extended surface (fins) of constant
cross section. One dimensional steady state heat conduction with uniform heat
generation, (plane wall and solid cylinder) critical radius of insulation. Concept of
unsteady state heat conduction. Transient heat flow system with negligible internal
resistance
Radiation
Nature of thermal radiation, definitions of absorptivity, reflectivity, transmissivity,
monochromatic emissive power, total emissive power and emissivity, concept of
black body and gray body, Kirchhoff laws, Wien’s law and Planck’s law, deduction
of Stefan Boltzmann equation. Lambert’s cosine rule, intensity of radiation, energy
III 9
change by radiation between two black surfaces with non-absorbing medium in
between and in absence of reradiating surfaces, geometric shape factor, energy
exchange by radiation between two gray surfaces without absorbing medium and
absence of radiation and radiosity, radiation network method, network for two
surfaces
Free Convection
Mass, momentum and energy conservation equations, non-dimensional numbers,
IV hydrodynamic and thermal boundary layers, basics of heat transfer in external and 6
internal laminar and turbulent flows, and use of co-relations. Free Convection and
use of its co-relations
Forced Convection
External flow: Thermal analysis of Flow over flat plate, cylinder, sphere and flow
V across tubes.
6
Internal flow: Convection correlations, Hydrodynamic and thermal considerations,
thermal analysis and convection correlations for circular and non-circular tubes.
Heat Exchangers
Exchangers, Tubular heat exchangers, Extended surface heat exchangers.
Classification according to flow arrangement. Fouling factor, mean temperature
difference, LMTD for parallel flow, counter flow, mean temperature for cross flow,
VI
correction factor, and special cases. The effectiveness by NTU method, effectiveness 5
of parallel, counter flow and cross flow heat exchangers and design consideration.
Heat pipe component and working principle.(Elementary treatment only) Types of
Heat exchangers

Course Objectives
1. To understand the fundamental principles of engineering mechanics and their interdisciplinary
applications.
2. To apply concepts of force, equilibrium, friction, stress, strain, and dynamics in engineering
systems.
3. To develop analytical and problem-solving skills relevant to Electrical Engineering applications.
4. To introduce students to modern engineering applications in renewable energy, EVs, robotics, and
smart systems.
5. To provide hands on practice for the conduct of experiments to verify the principles of mechanics
6. To demonstrate the graphical methods to verify analytical solutions

List of Laboratory Experiments
C Programming Experiments
1. Develop programs using variables, data types, operators, and formatted input-output functions
for engineering calculations.
2. Develop programs using if-else, nested if-else, and switch-case statements for solving
engineering problems.

multiplication, and transpose operations.

mathematical computations.
7. Implement programs using structures and pointers for handling engineering data.
8. Develop programs for reading, writing, and processing engineering data using files.
Python Programming Experiments

conversion.

calculations.
11. Develop programs using user-defined functions, recursion, and modular programming
concepts.
12. Implement programs using lists, tuples, dictionaries, and sets for data processing applications.
13. Develop programs for string manipulation and text file operations.
14. Perform array operations, matrix manipulations, and numerical computations using NumPy.
15. Generate and customize plots for engineering data and electrical waveforms.
16. Develop programs for waveform generation, RMS and power calculations, simple circuit
analysis, and electrical data visualization.

List of Experiments / Lab Activities/Topics
List of Lab Activities:
1. Implementation of electrical circuits in software tool PSpice to measure current and voltage in D.C.
circuit.
2. Verification of voltage and current division rule using hardware circuit.
3. Verification of Superposition Theorem to measure current and voltage in electrical circuit using
hardware and validate the result using software tool PSpice.
4. Verification of Thevenin’s Theorem to obtain equivalent circuit using hardware and validate the result
using software tool PSpice.
5. Verification of Norton’s Theorem to obtain equivalent circuit using hardware and validate the result
using software tool PSpice.
6. Determine transient and steady state behaviour of a first order circuit (R-C circuit) on hardware and
validate the results using software tool PSpice.
7. Determine transient and steady state behaviour of a second order circuit (R-L-C circuit) using software
tool PSpice.
8. Demonstration of transient and steady state(underdamped and overdamped) behaviour of a second
order circuit(R-L-C circuit) on hardware.
9. Implementation of electrical circuits in software tool PSpice to measure current and voltage in A.C.
circuit.
10. Determine the active power of a A.C. circuit using software tool PSpice.

List of Experiments / Lab Activities/Topics
The Community Engagement Project/Field Project integrates academic learning with community service,
allowing Electrical Engineering (EE) students to apply their technical skills in real-world settings. This course
aims to provide social responsibility, enhance problem-solving skills, and provide practical experience through
direct involvement in community projects.
List of Community Engagement Project / Field Project Activities:
1. Solar Power Installation for Community Centres: Design and install solar panels for local schools,
libraries, or community centres to provide them with sustainable energy solutions.
2. Energy Audits for Local Homes and Businesses: Conduct energy audits to help residents and
businesses identify ways to reduce energy consumption and costs.
3. Smart Lighting Systems: Develop and install smart lighting solutions for public parks or community
areas to enhance energy efficiency and safety.
4. Water Purification Systems: Create and implement water purification systems in areas with limited
access to clean drinking water.
5. Public Wi-Fi Networks: Set up free Wi-Fi hotspots in underserved areas to help bridge the digital
divide.
6. Electric Vehicle Charging Stations: Design and install EV charging stations in public spaces to
encourage the use of electric vehicles.
Course Contents for S. Y. B. Tech. Electrical Engineering Programme, Department of Electrical Engineering, AY 2024-25

7. Assistive Technology for Disabled Individuals: Create custom electronic devices or systems to aid
individuals with disabilities in the community.
8. Renewable Energy Workshops: Conduct workshops on building small-scale renewable energy
projects, like wind turbines or solar chargers, to educate and empower the community.
9. Smart Irrigation Systems: Design and implement smart irrigation systems for community gardens or
local farms to optimize water usage and improve crop yields.
10. E-Waste Recycling Program: Set up a program to collect and properly recycle electronic waste,
educating the community on the importance of e-waste management.
11. Home Automation for Elderly: Install simple home automation systems for elderly residents to
enhance their safety and convenience.
*Note- Students must deliver a final presentation and submit a comprehensive report as the end of their project.
The final presentation should be a concise, visually engaging slide deck that includes an introduction,
methodology, results with data visualizations, discussion, and conclusion, followed by a Q&A session to
address audience queries. Concurrently, students must submit a detailed report that documents every aspect of
their project from start to finish. This report should adhere to the specified guidelines and include sections such
as the title page, abstract, introduction, methodology, results, discussion, and conclusion, providing in-depth
information and supporting evidence for the project's findings.

Stage I shall be conducted after the First Year with a duration of 3–4 weeks carrying 2 credits. During this

develop professional competency, workplace awareness, technical understanding, and analytical abilities
relevant to engineering practice.
Stage II shall be conducted after the Second Year with a duration of 3–4 weeks carrying 2 credits. During this
stage, students are required to complete 120 hours of internship/training covering Design & Development of
Solutions, Investigation, and Modern Tool Usage to strengthen engineering design practices, problem-solving
abilities, and the effective application of modern engineering tools and technologies. Students can work in local
industry and solve real life industry problems by applying domain knowledge. A student can also take an in-
house internship offered by IIE cell, departmental research work, departmental in-house problem statement
under the faculty guidance.
Stage III shall be carried out after TY ESE with a minimum duration of 8 weeks carrying 4 credits. During this
stage, students are required to complete 120 hours of internship in the industry of their program domain. The
student can complete the internship in the industry in either 7th or 8th semester. Based on the criteria defined
by CDC cell, a student can undertake an internship of one year span during the entire 7th and 8th semester.
 Successful completion of all internship stages is mandatory for the award of credits and fulfilment of degree
requirements.
 The internship performance shall be evaluated based on internship report submission, presentation/viva-voce,
industry mentor feedback, completion of prescribed modules, and attainment of the defined course outcomes.

Mini Project Description:
A mini project shall be undertaken by a group consisting of three to four students. The project should involve
the design, development, construction, testing, and debugging of an electronic system approved by the
department. Each student is expected to actively participate in conceiving, designing, and developing the
idea that leads to the final project or product. The project theme should be relevant to the Electronics
Engineering discipline. The mini project is expected to be based on the foundational courses studied up
to the fourth semester of the B. Tech. programme, such as Electronic Circuit Analysis and Design, Digital
Systems and Microprocessors, Electronic Instrumentation, Data Structures and Algorithms Lab, Integrated
Circuits and Applications, Microcontroller Peripherals and Interfacing, Communication Engineering, and
Python Programming. The project should provide students with an opportunity to apply theoretical
knowledge and practical skills to develop innovative and effective engineering solutions.
Every student must maintain a project notebook/logbook to document the progress of the mini project,
including planning, design, implementation, testing, observations, and outcomes. The project
notebook/logbook will be reviewed periodically throughout the semester as a part of the continuous in-
semester evaluation process. At the end of the semester, each group is required to submit a soft-bound project
report detailing the objectives, methodology, design procedures, implementation, results, and conclusions of
the project. Furthermore, the final working product or prototype developed as part of the mini project
must be demonstrated during the examination, showcasing its functionality, performance, and
practical applicability.

Minor Project Description:
A Minor Project group shall normally consist of three to four students. The project involves identifying a
real-world societal or industrial problem and developing an innovative electronic system approved by the
department. Students are expected to conceive, design, implement, test, and demonstrate a functional
prototype by applying engineering principles and modern development tools.
The Minor Project provides an opportunity to integrate the knowledge and practical skills acquired up to the
fifth semester of the Electronics Engineering programme. Students should apply concepts from core subjects
such as analog and digital electronics, microcontrollers, instrumentation, communication, embedded
systems, and programming to develop a product-oriented solution.
The project shall follow a systematic engineering design process, including problem identification, literature
survey, requirement analysis, system design, hardware and software development, testing, validation, and
documentation. Emphasis shall be given to innovation, teamwork, technical competency, and practical
problem-solving.
Each student shall maintain an individual Project Logbook to record weekly progress and project activities.
The logbook will be reviewed periodically as a part of the continuous assessment. At the end of the semester,

Lab Activities/Topics
Students are required to complete the Internship Course in three stages distributed across the duration of the
undergraduate program, as prescribed by the curriculum.
I. Stage I shall be conducted after the completion of the First Year and shall have a duration of 3 to 4
weeks, carrying 2 academic credits. During this stage, students shall complete a minimum of 120
hours of internship/training focused on Industry Orientation, Professional Skills, Soft Skills,
Engineering Knowledge, and Problem Analysis. The primary objective of this training is to enhance
students' professional competence, workplace awareness, technical proficiency, and analytical
abilities required for effective engineering practice.
II. Stage-II shall be conducted after the completion of the Second Year and shall have a duration of 3
to 4 weeks, carrying 2 academic credits. During this stage, students shall complete a minimum of
120 hours of internship/training focusing on Design and Development of Solutions, Investigation,
and the Use of Modern Engineering Tools. The objective of this training is to strengthen students'
engineering design capabilities, problem-solving skills, and proficiency in the effective application
of contemporary engineering tools and technologies. Students may undertake internships in local
industries and work on real-world industrial problems by applying their domain knowledge.
Alternatively, students may opt for in-house internship opportunities offered by the Innovation,
Incubation and Entrepreneurship (IIE) Cell, participate in departmental research projects, or work
on departmental problem statements under the guidance of faculty members.
Course Contents for B. Tech. Programme, Department of Electronics Engineering, AY2026-27

III. Stage-III shall be undertaken after the completion of the Third Year End Semester Examination (TY
ESE) and shall have a minimum duration of eight weeks, carrying 4 academic credits. During this
stage, students are required to complete a minimum of 120 hours of internship training in an industry
relevant to their respective program domain. The internship may be undertaken during either the 7th
or 8th Semester. Furthermore, subject to the criteria and guidelines prescribed by the Career
Development Cell (CDC), a student may undertake an extended internship spanning the entire
duration of the Seventh and Eighth Semesters, up to a maximum period of one year. The objective
of this stage is to provide students with substantial industry exposure, enable the application of
theoretical knowledge to real-world engineering challenges, and enhance their professional,
technical, and organizational competencies.
 Successful completion of all internship stages is mandatory for the award of academic
credits and the fulfilment of the requirements for the award of the degree.
 The performance of students during the internship shall be evaluated on the basis of the
submission and quality of the internship report, presentation and viva-voce examination,
feedback received from the industry mentor, successful completion of the prescribed
training modules, and the extent of attainment of the specified course outcomes.

List of Experiments / Lab Activities
List of Experiments:
1. To familiarize with Computer and Mobile System Components and Operating
Systems.
Procedure:
● Identify and label the major hardware components of a computer system and mobile
device.
● Discuss the function of each component and its role in system operation.
● Ask students to identify and label of each component correctly.
● Discuss the function of each component and its role in the computer system.
● Explore the basic features of desktop and mobile operating systems

2. To understand the interaction between hardware and software for I/O
operations.
Procedure:
● Introduce students to a simple I/O operation, such as reading input from the
keyboard.
● Discuss the hardware components involved in the process, including the
keyboard controller and CPU.
● Demonstrate how the software interacts with hardware to perform the I/O operation.
3. To introduce students to the fundamentals of Operating systems.
Procedure:
● Set up multiple computers with different operating systems
(Computer-Windows, macOS, Linux. & Mobile- Android, ios).
● Ask students to perform basic tasks on each system, such as file management and
software installation.
● Compare and contrast the features and interfaces of different operating
systems.
4. To understand the components and functions of a CPU.
Procedure:
● Disassemble a CPU to show its internal components, such as ALU, control
unit, and registers.
● Explain the function of each component and how they work together to
execute instructions.
● Demonstrate a simple instruction execution process using a simulator.
5. To explore the performance of different levels of memory hierarchy.
Procedure:
● Use a benchmarking tool to measure the access time of RAM, cache, and
virtual memory.
● Compare the performance results of each memory level and discuss the
trade-offs.
● Analyze the impact of cache hits and misses on program execution time
6. To familiarize students with the anatomy of a motherboard.
Procedure:
● Show a motherboard diagram highlighting various components and
connectors.
● Ask students to identify each component and explain its purpose.
● Demonstrate the installation of hardware components like RAM and
expansion cards.
7. To explore the components of a graphics card and their functions.
Procedure:
● Disassemble a graphics card to show its GPU, VRAM, and other
components.
● Explain the role of each component in processing and rendering graphics.
● Demonstrate basic GPU-accelerated tasks using graphics software.
8. To compare different display technologies.
Procedure:
● Set up a computer system with displays using different technologies (CRT,
LCD, LED, etc.).

● Observe and compare the image quality, resolution,
and power consumption of each display type.
● Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of each display technology.
9. To set up a simple LAN and understand basic networking components.
Procedure:
● Provide networking equipment like switches and Ethernet cables.
● Ask students to connect multiple computers to form a LAN.
● Verify network connectivity and communication between connected devices.
10. To understand the role of ports and protocols in networking.
Procedure:
● Introduce students to different network protocols (TCP, UDP) and port
numbers.
● Use network monitoring tools to analyze network traffic and identify the protocols
used.
● Demonstrate the establishment of a connection between a client and server using
specific protocols.
11. To teach students common hardware troubleshooting techniques.
Procedure:
● Intentionally create hardware issues like loose connections or faulty
components in a computer.
● Ask students to diagnose and resolve these issues using appropriate
troubleshooting tools.
● Discuss the troubleshooting process and best practices.
12. To understand the importance of computer security and antivirus.
Procedure:
● Set up a computer with various types of malware (simulated or isolated) on it.
● Install an antivirus program and demonstrate malware scanning and
removal.
● Discuss the importance of keeping antivirus software up to date and
practicing safe computing habits
13. Case study of Data Center.
Procedure:
● Selecting any data center for study.
● Study the components of data center.
● If possible, visit to the data center.

List of Lab Activities:
Students will be given hands-on experience to design and implement efficient and effective
algorithms for various problems based on the syllabus covered in the course Computer
Algorithms in the Practical hours using any suitable programming language like C, C++, Java.
The List of experiments may include 12 to 14 experiments from among the following-
1. Write a program that solves recurrence relations using the master method. Accept input in the
form T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n) and determine time complexity.
2. To implement a sorting and searching algorithms using an array as a data structure and analyze its
time complexity for different values of n. The large number of elements may be generated using a
Random Number generator or may be stored in a file. (Quick Sort, Merge Sort, Linear, Binary,
Binary recursive)
3. To implement the Fractional Knapsack problem and activity selection problem using Greedy
method.
4. Find the Minimum Cost Spanning Tree of a given undirected graph using Kruskal's & Prim’s
algorithm and compare.
5. To apply the Greedy method to solve problems of
a) Job sequencing with deadlines
b) Optimal storage on tapes
6. Implement the following using Dynamic Programming
a) Matrix-chain multiplication
b) Longest common subsequence
c) Optimal binary search trees
d) Rod Cutting Problem
7. To implement Strassen’s matrix multiplication algorithm
8. From a given vertex in a weighted connected graph, find shortest paths to other vertices using
Dijkstra's algorithm.
9. Find a subset of a given set S = {s1,s2,.....,sn} of n positive integers whose sum is equal to a given
positive integer d. For example, if S= {1, 2, 5, 6, 8} and d = 9 there are two solutions {1,2,6} and
{1,8}. A suitable message is to be displayed if the given problem instance doesn't have a solution.
10. Implement any scheme to find the optimal solution for the Traveling Salesperson problem and
then solve the same problem instance using any approximation algorithm and determine the error
in the approximation.
11. Implement the following using Back Tracking
a) 8-Queen's problem
b) Hamiltonian cycle
c) Graph coloring Problem
12. Implement All-Pairs Shortest Paths Problem using Floyd's algorithm. Parallelize this algorithm by
creating multiple threads and determine the speed-up achieved.
13. Compare and evaluate the performance of different Randomization and Approximation
algorithms

Desired Requisites: Physics, Mathematics
Teaching Scheme Examination Scheme (Marks)
Lecture 2 Hrs/week MSE ESE LA Total
Tutorials -- 20 50 30 100
Practical 2 Hrs/week Credits: 3
Course Objectives
1. To impart the fundamentals of engineering mechanics related to force systems, equilibrium, mass properties, motion and
energy of particles and rigid bodies.
2. To develop the ability to apply principles of statics, kinematics and kinetics to analyse simple engineering and robotic
mechanical systems.
3. To provide hands-on experience in experimental verification, measurement and interpretation of fundamental mechanics
principles.
4. To illustrate the relevance of engineering mechanics to robotic links, joints, actuators, grippers and mobile robotic
platforms.
Course Outcomes (CO) with Bloom’s Taxonomy Level
At the end of the course, the students will be able to,
Bloom’s Bloom’s
CO Course Outcome Statement/s Taxonomy Taxonomy
Level Description
Explain the fundamental principles of force systems, equilibrium, mass properties,
CO1 II Understanding
kinematics and kinetics of particles and rigid bodies.
Apply principles of statics and kinematics to determine forces, moments, reactions,
CO2 position, velocity and acceleration in simple engineering and robotic mechanical III Applying
systems.
Analyze particle and fixed-axis rigid-body motion using force-acceleration, work-
CO3 energy and impulse-momentum principles to determine force, torque, energy and IV Analyzing
power requirements.
Analyze experimental data from engineering mechanics activities to verify
CO4 principles and compare observed behaviour with theoretical predictions for simple IV Analyzing
mechanical and robotic systems.
Module Module Contents Hours
Force Systems and Free-Body Diagrams: Concept of particle and rigid body; scalars and
vectors; force representation and Cartesian components; composition and resolution of
concurrent and non-concurrent coplanar force systems; resultants; moments and couples;
I 5
equivalent force-couple system; Varignon's theorem; free-body diagrams, supports, contacts and
mechanical joint forces. Introductory three-dimensional force vector and moment interpretation
using M = r x F.
Equilibrium, Friction and Simple Engineering Structures: Equilibrium of two-dimensional
rigid bodies; two-force and three-force bodies; simple connected bodies; roller, pin and fixed
supports; beam loads and support reactions. Dry friction, static and kinetic friction, limiting
II 5
friction, coefficient and angle of friction; impending motion; applications to blocks, inclined
planes, simple wedges and belts. Introductory analysis of simple statically determinate plane
trusses by method of joints and method of sections.

Centroid, Centre of Mass, Moment of Inertia and Virtual Work: Centroid of lines and
simple/composite plane areas; centre of mass and centre of gravity. Area moment of inertia of
III simple and composite sections; parallel-axis theorem and radius of gyration. Mass moment of 4
inertia of common rigid bodies; parallel-axis theorem and effect of mass distribution. Principle
of virtual work and equilibrium of simple mechanical systems.
Kinematics of Particles and Rigid Bodies: Position, displacement, velocity and acceleration;
rectilinear and curvilinear motion; graphical interpretation of motion; normal-tangential
IV components; elementary projectile motion; relative motion of particles in translating frames. 5
Rigid-body translation and fixed-axis rotation; angular displacement, velocity and acceleration;
relations v = rω, a_t = rα and a_n = rω².
Kinetics of Particles and Rigid Bodies: Newton's laws of motion; equations of motion using F
= ma in Cartesian and normal-tangential forms; motion on smooth and rough surfaces; simple
V connected bodies; introductory D'Alembert's principle. Translation and fixed-axis rotation of 5
rigid bodies; torque-angular acceleration relation ΣM = Iα; simple applications involving
payloads, rotating links and actuators.
Work-Energy, Impulse-Momentum and Engineering Applications: Work of forces and
couples; kinetic energy of particles and rigid bodies in translation and fixed-axis rotation;
gravitational and elastic potential energy; work-energy principle and conservation of mechanical
VI 4
energy. Power and efficiency; P = Fv and P = τω. Linear impulse-momentum and conservation
of momentum; introductory angular impulse-momentum; direct central impact and coefficient of
restitution. Applications to simple robotic and mechanical systems.
Total Theory Contact Hours: 28
List of Experiments / Lab Activities
Verification of equilibrium of concurrent coplanar force systems using free-body diagrams, analytical resolution and
1)
experimental force measurements.
2) Verification of the principle of moments and determination of support reactions for a simply supported member.
Determination of coefficient of friction on horizontal and inclined planes and application to impending motion, gripping or
3)
wheel traction.
Experimental determination of centroid / centre of mass of a simple composite or irregular body and comparison with
4)
analytical prediction.
5) Experimental determination of mass moment of inertia of a rigid body and study of the effect of mass distribution.
6) Verification of the principle of virtual work using a simple lever, pulley or mechanical linkage system.
Experimental study of particle kinematics: determination of displacement, velocity and acceleration from measured motion
7)
data.
Experimental study of fixed-axis rotational kinematics: determination of angular displacement, angular velocity and angular
8)
acceleration; verification of v = rω.
9) Verification of Newton's second law for translational motion and the force-acceleration relationship F = ma.
10) Experimental study of fixed-axis rotational kinetics and the torque-angular acceleration relationship ΣM = Iα.
Verification of the work-energy principle and estimation of mechanical power in a simple translating, lifting or rotating
11)
system.
12) Experimental study of impact / collision and determination of coefficient of restitution using a suitable apparatus.
Integrative R&A mechanics activity using measured parameters to analyse a simple gripper, wheel-drive, payload-lifting or
13)
single-link rotational system.
Equivalent experiment / mini activity aligned with the course outcomes may be included based on available equipment and
14)
laboratory facilities.

Beer, F. P., Johnston, E. R., Mazurek, D. F. et al., Vector Mechanics for Engineers: Statics and Dynamics, McGraw-Hill

Education.

List of Experiments / Lab Activities/Topics

1. Workshop Safety, Hand Tools, Fasteners and Basic Assembly Practices
2. Basic Cutting, Fitting, Drilling and Finishing Operations
3. Study and Demonstration of Conventional Machine Tools and Cutting Machines
4. Sheet-Metal Fabrication, Bending and Mechanical Joining
