1. Workshop Safety, Hand Tools, Fasteners and Basic Assembly Practices
Details / Scope: Workshop rules and safe working practices; PPE; safe handling and correct use of spanners, Allen keys,
screwdrivers, pliers, hammers, files, hacksaws, punches and similar hand tools; types and applications of bolts, nuts,
washers, machine screws, socket-head screws and grub screws; clearance and threaded holes; correct tightening, assembly
and dismantling practices.
Expected Hands-on Activity: Identify common tools and fasteners, select the appropriate tool for a given operation, and
perform assembly/disassembly of a simple mechanical unit using safe practices.
2. Basic Cutting, Fitting, Drilling and Finishing Operations
Details / Scope: Marking and layout using steel rule, scriber, try-square, divider and center punch; hacksaw cutting; basic
filing techniques and types of files; drilling-machine safety; drill selection; drilling and countersinking; introduction to tapping
where facilities permit; deburring and surface finishing.
Expected Hands-on Activity: Demonstration only.
3. Study and Demonstration of Conventional Machine Tools and Cutting Machines
Details / Scope: Construction, basic working principle, applications and safety of lathe, drilling machine, bench grinder,
power hacksaw/band saw/circular saw or available stock-cutting equipment; work holding and cutting tools; demonstration
of facing, simple straight turning, drilling and stock-cutting operations; qualitative introduction to cutting speed and feed.
Expected Hands-on Activity: Observe guided demonstrations, identify major machine components, and record the
sequence from workpiece holding and tool setting to machining/cutting and the finished component. Independent advanced
machine operation is not expected.
4. Sheet-Metal Fabrication, Bending and Mechanical Joining
Details / Scope: Identification of commonly used sheet materials and thicknesses; safe handling of sheet metal and sharp
edges; marking and layout; cutting using hand shears/snips or suitable available equipment; drilling/punching; basic bending
and forming; introductory bend radius/bend allowance; riveting and other mechanical joining methods; detachable joints
using screws/fasteners; deburring and finishing.
Expected Hands-on Activity: Demonstration only.
5. Study and Demonstration of CNC Machining and Laser Cutting
Details / Scope: Introduction to digital manufacturing; conventional versus CNC machining; basic CNC axes and coordinate
system; CAD-CAM-toolpath-simulation-machining workflow; work holding, cutting-tool selection and introductory feed,
speed and depth of cut. Laser-cutting principle; suitable materials; 2D CAD/vector/DXF profiles; cutting and engraving; kerf;
nesting; basic process parameters and safety.
Expected Hands-on Activity: Observe CNC machining of a simple component/profile and laser cutting of a simple
plate/bracket/profile, including preparation, machine setup and processing; compare the capabilities and typical
applications of the two processes.
6. Basic Fabrication by Arc Welding, Grinding and Finishing
Details / Scope: Welding safety and PPE; basic principle of arc welding; welding machine, electrode, electrode holder and
earth connection; workpiece preparation and positioning; simple lap or butt joint; introductory identification of common
visible weld defects; grinding-machine safety, deburring, grinding and finishing; typical applications in frames, supports and
fixtures.
Expected Hands-on Activity: Under supervision, Demonstration only.

7. Dimensional Measurement and Inspection of Manufactured Components
Details / Scope: Importance of measurement and inspection; least count and selection of a suitable instrument; use of
Vernier caliper, outside micrometer, depth-measuring facility/gauge, feeler gauge, thread pitch gauge and radius gauge.
Expected Hands-on Activity: Measure suitable features of engineering components (simple geometries to cover diameter,
length, width, height, etc.) and prepare an inspection sheet showing specified/nominal dimension, measuring instrument,
measured dimension.
8. Electrical Safety, Basic Wiring and Measurement Using Electrical Instruments
Details / Scope: Electrical laboratory safety; introductory distinction between AC and DC; polarity, voltage, current and
resistance in practical measurements; digital multimeter functions, terminal/range selection and continuity testing;
regulated DC power supply; switches, fuses/protection devices and terminal blocks; basic series and parallel connections
and safe low-voltage wiring.
Expected Hands-on Activity: Measure voltage and resistance; perform continuity checks; identify polarity; verify wiring
using a digital multimeter and DC power supply; identify simple connection faults.
9. Basic Electronic Components, Breadboarding and Circuit Testing
Details / Scope: Identification and basic function of resistor, capacitor, diode, LED, transistor, pushbutton/switch,
potentiometer, buzzer and relay; resistor color code; polarized and non-polarized components; breadboard internal
connections; simple LED and switching circuits; introductory transistor/relay switching concept; circuit testing using a
multimeter. Detailed semiconductor theory is outside the scope.
Expected Hands-on Activity: Identify basic electronic components and assemble simple breadboard circuits such as LED
indication, pushbutton-controlled LED/buzzer, transistor switching or relay-based output; test and verify circuit operation.
10. Soldering, Desoldering, Wire Preparation, Crimping and Connector Practices
Details / Scope: Soldering-iron safety; selection and preparation of wire; stripping and conductor preparation; tinning;
correct soldering technique and identification of satisfactory/poor solder joints; basic desoldering; crimp terminals and
crimping tools; common connectors and terminal blocks; heat-shrink tubing; cable routing and basic cable-management
practices; continuity testing.
Expected Hands-on Activity: Hands-on practice with soldering and desoldering activity

Experiments should be based on following course contents

List of Experiments / Lab Activities
1. Course orientation, artefact-vs-application framing, team formation, selection of an artefact-based need
statement/theme, and mentor allocation.
2. Problem definition, measurable requirements and success metrics; preparation of the Foundation
Integration Map linking major design decisions to foundational courses.
3. Generation and comparison of system concepts; development of the complete system architecture,
subsystem interfaces, and Review Gate 1 presentation.
Course Contents for T Y B. Tech. Programme, Department of Robotics & Automation AY 2026-27

4. Mechanical design and engineering calculations including load, force, torque, stress,
material/component selection, and appropriate safety margins.
5. CAD assembly modelling, drawings, tolerances/clearances, BOM and manufacturability; actuator,
drive and sensor sizing with predicted performance values.
6. Electronics, signal-chain and embedded/control planning: driver/interface circuits, I/O plan, signal
conditioning, PID/state-machine/trajectory approach, and design finalization (LA1).
7. Fabrication/prototyping and parallel implementation of mechanical, sensing, actuation and embedded
subsystems; calibration and independent subsystem testing.
8. Subsystem implementation review using measured test data; maintenance of a formal debugging log
recording symptom, test, root cause, correction, and learning.
9. System integration and validation against defined requirements; predicted-vs-measured comparison,
quantified error analysis, and at least one documented improvement/re-test cycle.
10. Final consolidation: working artefact demonstration, complete technical report and logbook, minimum
three root-cause debugging cycles, individual viva, and reflection on foundational-course integration.
Indicative artefact themes: 3-DOF Robotic Arm; Closed-Loop Drive System; Fluid-Power Positioning
System; Force-Modulated Gripper; Precision Positioning Table; Dead-Reckoning Localization System.
Equivalent artefact-based themes may be approved when aligned with the course objectives.

To introduce the hardware wiring, configuration, and practical execution of hardwired relay logic

List of Experiments / Lab Activities
1. Relay Logic Control: Demonstration and hardwired development of basic relay logic circuits (AND,
OR, NOT logic using physical relays).
2. Motor Control & Latching: Design and implementation of a motor start-stop circuit with latching
(sealing) logic using both hardwired components and PLC software.
3. Traffic Control System: Development and execution of timer-based ladder logic for a multi-way road
crossing traffic light sequence.
4. Tank water Level Management: Programming a water level controller using sensor inputs to
sequence inlet/outlet pumps and trigger alarms based on level thresholds.
5. Elevator Control Sequence: Programming the logic for a multi-floor lift/elevator system, utilizing
limit switches, door timers, and floor call memory blocks.
6. Vending Machine Logic: Development of a program using up/down counters and data comparators to
simulate vending machine operation (coin counting and product dispensing).
7. Automated Object Detection: Wiring and programming logic to differentiate objects using a
combination of inductive, capacitive, and photoelectric sensors.
8. Conveyor Control System: Integrating digital sensors to sequence a material handling conveyor (start,
stop on detection, and batch counting).

9. Electro-Pneumatic Sequence Control: Programming a multi-cylinder cascade sequence (e.g., A+ B+
A- B-) using PLC outputs to trigger solenoid valves and reed switches for positional feedback.
10. Automated Sorting Station: Integrating sensors and pneumatic cylinders on a gravity chute to sort
metallic and non-metallic materials into respective bins.
11. VFD Interfacing: Connecting a PLC to a Variable Frequency Drive (VFD) to control the speed and
direction of a 3-phase AC motor via digital and analog signals.
12. HMI Integration: Programming an industrial Human Machine Interface (HMI) screen to monitor
PLC data tags, start/stop a process, and display machine fault alarms.
13. Robotic Pick-and-Place Workcell Simulation: Simulating the sequence logic, safety interlocks, and
hardware handshake signals required between a PLC and a robotic manipulator.

Minor Project Description:
The Minor Project is intended as a progression from the Semester V Mini Project. Students shall carry
forward the practices of requirement definition, design-before-build, subsystem integration, quantitative
validation, systematic debugging, and technical documentation, with greater emphasis on application
context, stakeholder/user needs, engineering realization, and demonstrable utility.
A Minor Project group shall normally consist of three to four students. The project may address a new
approved problem or may substantially extend earlier Mini Project work. Problems may originate from
industry, society, research laboratories, faculty, student innovation, competitions, or other relevant sources.
Interaction with industry, end users, research organizations, or external mentors may be undertaken
wherever appropriate and feasible, while student ownership of the engineering work shall remain essential.
The project scope may include robotic or mechatronic systems, automation subsystems/cells, mobile
robots, manipulators and end-effectors, machine-vision or sensing-enabled systems,
embedded/control/software solutions, or other suitable Robotics and Automation applications. The
expected outcome may be a functional prototype, validated proof-of-concept, integrated demonstrator, or
equivalent engineering realization appropriate to the approved scope. The project shall follow a systematic
engineering process including problem identification, literature/existing-solution study, requirements,
Course Contents for T Y B. Tech. Programme, Department of Robotics & Automation AY 2026-27

concept and feasibility assessment, system architecture, modelling/calculations and design,
implementation, subsystem testing, integration, validation, iteration, and documentation. Performance shall
be evaluated against defined requirements rather than only by visual demonstration.
Each team shall plan milestones and responsibilities and maintain relevant design records, resource/BOM
and cost details as applicable, test data, and review evidence. Each student shall maintain an individual
Project Logbook to record weekly progress, contribution, observations, and learning. The logbook shall be
reviewed periodically as part of continuous assessment. At the end of the semester, each team shall submit
a project report in the prescribed format and present/demonstrate the completed work during the End
Semester Examination.

List of Topics (Applicable for Interaction Mode):
1. Problem Solving and C Programming Fundamentals: Introduction to problem solving, algorithms,
flowcharts, pseudocode, programming languages, features and structure of C, variables, constants, data types,
operators, expressions, input/output functions, C program compilation process, different stages of
compilation and intermediate files generated, code size measurement, and basic memory organization
of a C program.
2. Control Statements and Functions: Decision-making statements (if, if-else, nested if, switch), looping
statements (while, do-while, for), break and continue, functions, recursion, parameter passing, scope, storage
classes and their memory implications.
3.Arrays, Strings and Pointers: One-dimensional and two-dimensional arrays, strings and string handling
functions, introduction to pointers, pointer arithmetic, arrays and pointers, dynamic memory allocation, C
memory map, memory organization of variables and data.
4. Structures, File Handling and Introduction to Data Structures: Structures, arrays of structures, unions,
file handling, overview of data structures, classification of linear and non-linear data structures, asymptotic
notation (Big-O concept), searching (Linear and Binary Search) and sorting (Bubble, Selection and Insertion
Sort).
5.Linear Data Structures: Arrays as data structures, linked lists (singly linked list), stacks and queues,
implementation using arrays and linked lists, applications.
6.Introduction to Non-Linear Data Structures: Trees: terminology, binary tree, binary search tree (concept
and basic operations), Graphs: terminology, graph representations (adjacency matrix and adjacency list),
applications of trees and graphs.

List of Experiments / Lab Activities/Topics
The Community Engagement Project/Field Project integrates academic learning with community service,
allowing Electrical Engineering (EE) students to apply their technical skills in real-world settings. This
course aims to provide social responsibility, enhance problem-solving skills, and provide practical experience
through direct involvement in community projects.
List of Community Engagement Project / Field Project Activities:
1. Solar Power Installation for Community Centres: Design and install solar panels for local schools,
libraries, or community centres to provide them with sustainable energy solutions.
2. Energy Audits for Local Homes and Businesses: Conduct energy audits to help residents and
businesses identify ways to reduce energy consumption and costs.
3. Smart Lighting Systems: Develop and install smart lighting solutions for public parks or community
areas to enhance energy efficiency and safety.
4. Water Purification Systems: Create and implement water purification systems in areas with limited
access to clean drinking water.
5. Public Wi-Fi Networks: Set up free Wi-Fi hotspots in underserved areas to help bridge the digital
divide.
6. Electric Vehicle Charging Stations: Design and install EV charging stations in public spaces to
encourage the use of electric vehicles.

7. Assistive Technology for Disabled Individuals: Create custom electronic devices or systems to aid
individuals with disabilities in the community.
8. Renewable Energy Workshops: Conduct workshops on building small-scale renewable energy
projects, like wind turbines or solar chargers, to educate and empower the community.
9. Smart Irrigation Systems: Design and implement smart irrigation systems for community gardens or
local farms to optimize water usage and improve crop yields.
10. E-Waste Recycling Program: Set up a program to collect and properly recycle electronic waste,
educating the community on the importance of e-waste management.
11. Home Automation for Elderly: Install simple home automation systems for elderly residents to
enhance their safety and convenience.
*Note- Students must deliver a final presentation and submit a comprehensive report as the end of their
project. The final presentation should be a concise, visually engaging slide deck that includes an introduction,
methodology, results with data visualizations, discussion, and conclusion, followed by a Q&A session to
address audience queries. Concurrently, students must submit a detailed report that documents every aspect
of their project from start to finish. This report should adhere to the specified guidelines and include sections
such as the title page, abstract, introduction, methodology, results, discussion, and conclusion, providing in-
depth information and supporting evidence for the project's findings.

Evaluation (ISE), and End-Semester Examination (ESE). A formative assessment approach shall be adopted
throughout the course.

be assigned to the students as part of the assessment process.

In-Semester Evaluation (ISE): The ISE shall be conducted throughout the semester based on continuous
teacher assessment. The modes of evaluation may include activities such as Objective type question-answer,
peer review, Group discussion, assignments, participation, reflective writing etc.
End-Semester Examination (ESE): The ESE shall cover all modules of the course, with approximately
40% weightage assigned to Modules 1 and 2 and 60% weightage assigned to Modules 3 to 5. The ESE shall
be conducted in the form of an Oral Examination and Presentation.
Passing Criteria:
To successfully complete the course, a student must secure:
A minimum of 40% marks in the aggregate of MSE, ISE, and ESE, and A minimum of 40% marks in the
ESE separately, as the ESE shall constitute a separate head of passing.

Course Code 7CV204
Course Name Concrete Technology
Desired Requisites: -
Teaching Scheme Examination Scheme (Marks)
Lecture 3 Hrs/week MSE ISE ESE Total
Tutorial - 30 20 50 100
Credits: 3
Course Objectives
1 To impart conceptual knowledge of cement, cement concrete, aggregates and admixtures.
2 To make students conversant with fresh and hardened properties and durability issues of concrete.
3 To provide and develop skills to prepare and design concrete mixes.
Course Outcomes (CO)
At the end of the course, the students will be able to,
Blooms Taxonomy
CO Description
Descriptor Level
Perceive the knowledge of cement, aggregate, admixtures and concrete to
CO1 Understand II
fulfil the requirements of the construction industry.
Articulate the process of manufacturing concrete, and demonstrate properties
CO2 Apply III
of fresh concrete.
Apply the knowledge of the properties of hardened concrete and the
CO3 Apply III
durability issues of concrete.
CO4 Design concrete mixes according to IS 10262: 2019 codal provisions. Design VI
Module Module Contents Hrs
Ingredients of Concrete 7
Cement: Manufacturing of Portland cement, Chemical composition, Hydration of cement,
Classification and types of cement, Tests on cement.
I
Aggregate: Classification, Mechanical and Physical Properties, Grading of Aggregates,
Tests on aggregate, Artificial and recycled aggregate.
Water - Mixing Water and Curing Water
Concrete Manufacturing Process 7
Mixing, Transportation, Placing, compaction and finishing.
II
Admixtures: Introduction to Mineral and Chemical Admixtures
Ready Mix Plant: Layout, Components and Functions, etc.
Properties of Fresh Concrete 6
Workability: Factors affecting workability, measurement of workability, Cohesion and
III
segregation, bleeding, and Setting of concrete.
Curing - Methods of curing
Concrete Mix Design 7
IV Factors to be considered, Concrete mix design for compressive strength by IS: 10262
(2019) method, Statistical quality control.
Properties of Hardened Concrete 8
Strength of concrete, factors affecting strength, Micro-cracking and stress-strain relation,
V Elasticity, tensile and flexural strength, Creep, and Shrinkage.
Non-destructive testing of concrete.
Durability: Fundamental Concepts, Degradation Process, Attacks, and Durability issues.
Special Concretes: High-Performance Concrete, Self-Compacting Concrete, Dry Lean 4
VI Concrete, Pavement Quality Concrete, Pre-stressed Concrete, Low Carbon footprint
concrete

Course Objectives
To introduce students to fundamental concepts of Limit state design of reinforced concrete structures using
1
IS 456:200.
To equip students with the skill of determining the strength of RCC members for different criteria of the
2
Limit state.
To provide knowledge and skills to students required for the design of basic RCC members using the IS
3
456:2000.
Course Outcomes (CO)
Blooms Taxonomy
CO Description
Descriptor Level
At the end of the course, the students will be able to,
CO1 Summarize design philosophies, material behaviour, and IS 456:2000 provisions
Understand II
on durability and load combinations.
CO2 Apply relevant clauses of IS 456:2000 for designing reinforced concrete structural
Apply III
elements.

Analyze IV
code.

CO4 Create VI
codal provisions.
Module Module Contents Hrs
I Fundamentals of Structural Design and Design Philosophies: 3
RCC Design Overview: Importance, applications, and structural behavior.
Design Methods: Working Stress, Ultimate Load, and Limit State Methods – concepts
and comparison.
Design Steps: Load types, combinations, structural system selection, analysis, and design
procedure.
Material Properties: Key properties and stress-strain behavior of concrete and steel.
IS 456:2000 Introduction: Code guidelines, safety factors, and design approach.
II Design of RC Beams: Part 1 9
Singly and Doubly Reinforced Beams: Stress block analysis, neutral axis depth, section
types (balanced, under-reinforced, over-reinforced), moment of resistance, design
procedure, effective length
Flanged Beams (T and L Sections): Types, effective flange width, stress block analysis,
moment of resistance, design steps
Course Contents for BTech Programme, Department of Civil Engineering,
AY2025-26 onwards

III Design of RC Beams: Part 2, Shear, Bond, and Torsion: 7
Shear: Shear stress distribution in isotropic and RC beams, truss analogy, critical shear
sections, IS code design provisions for shear
Bond: Bond stress, development length, standard hooks and anchorage details
Torsion: Equivalent shear and moment in RC members, design of beams for torsion as
per IS code
IV Design of RC Slabs and Staircases: 7
Types and behavior of slabs, Codal provisions for slabs, Design of one-way slabs: single span,
continuous, and cantilever, Design of two-way slabs using IS code method, Design of dog-
legged staircases.
V Design of RC Columns: 7
Types of columns: short & long, axially loaded & with bending, Effective length of
columns, IS 456 codal provisions, Load carrying capacity of axially loaded short and long
columns, Design of columns under combined axial load and uniaxial bending, P-M
interaction diagram.
VI Design of RC Footing: 6
Design of isolated footings: Square and Rectangular footing, Eccentric footing
Design of combined footings: Rectangular & Trapezoidal Combined Footing

The lab work shall consist of detailed design &drawing of the following R. C. structures
Part 1. Residential G+1 storey building
1. Forming groups of 4-5 students in each batch and choose a specific Residential RC structure
(G+1) with isolated footing to design.
2. Prepare detailed drawing of structure using AutoCAD.
3. Design structural element of RC structure. (Footing, Column, Beam, slab etc.)
4. Prepare detailed bar bending schedule for all structural elements.
5. Prepare detailed report of project.
Part 2. Residential G+1 Storey Building Design Using STAAD.Pro
1. Form groups of 4–5 students in each batch and select a specific Residential RC structure (G+1)
with isolated footing for structural design.
2. Create a 3D structural model of the building using STAAD.Pro, defining appropriate materials,
supports, and load cases.
3. Analyze and design RC structural elements such as footings, columns, beams, and slabs using
STAAD.Pro as per relevant design codes.
4. Generate and compile a detailed bar bending schedule for all structural elements based on the
analysis and design output.
5. Prepare a comprehensive project report including modeling steps, design results, bar bending
schedule, and conclusions.

Guidelines:
1. The mini-project is a team activity having 3-5 students in a team.
2. Mini project should include mainly Mechanical Engineering contents but can be
multi-disciplinary as well.
2. The mini project may be a complete hardware or a combination of hardware and software.
3. Mini Project should cater to a small system required in laboratory, repair, maintenance or
upgradation of existing laboratory equipment or solution for a real life problem/case study.
4. After interactions with batch teacher and based on comprehensive literature survey/ need
analysis, the student shall identify the title and define the aim and objectives of mini-project.
5. Student is expected to detail out specifications, methodology, resources required, critical issues
involved in design and implementation and submit the proposal within first week of the semester.
6. The student is expected to exert on design, development and testing of the proposed work as per
the schedule.
7. Completed mini project and documentation in the form of mini project report is to be submitted
at the end of semester.
Guidelines for Assessment of Mini Project Examination:
Each batch should prepare a detailed technical report as per the guidelines issued by the department /
guide.
Mini Project shall be assessed through a presentation and demonstration by the student project group to
faculty advisor / a panel of examiners.
Students shall be motivated to publish a paper based on the work in students competitions / Conferences /
journals.
Mini Project shall be assessed based on following points;
1. Quality of problem and clarity.
2. Proper use of knowledge and practices of mechanical and or other engineering disciplines.
3. Effective use of tools and skill sets.
4. Contribution of an individual’s as a team member.
5. Clarity in written and oral communication and preparation and presentation of final technical
report.

List of Lab Activities:

at intervals.

display it.
4. Ultrasonic Distance Sensor: Measure distance using an ultrasonic sensor and display it.
5. Servo Motor Control: Control the movement of a servo motor using potentiometers or
sensors.

7. Sound Reactive LEDs: Make LEDs react to sound using a microphone sensor.

or automation.

10. Data Logging: Log sensor data to an SD card and analyze it later.
11. Wireless Communication: Use modules like Bluetooth or Wi-Fi to communicate with other
devices or the internet.
12. Home Automation: Automate home appliances like lights, fans, etc., using relays and
sensors.
13. Gesture Control: Control devices using gestures detected by sensors like accelerometers or
gyroscopes.
14. RFID Access Control: Create an RFID-based access control system.
15. Weather Station: Measure temperature, humidity, and other weather parameters and
display them.
16. Robotics Projects: Build robots like line-following robots, obstacle avoidance robots, etc.,
using Arduino.
17. Pulse Rate Monitor: Use sensors to measure pulse rate and display it.
18. Smart Agriculture: Monitor soil moisture, temperature, etc., and automate irrigation
systems.
19. GPS Tracker: Track location using GPS modules.
20. Touch-based Interfaces: Create touch-sensitive interfaces using capacitive touch sensors.

List of Experiments

and verify connectivity using ping and traceroute commands.)
2. Exploring Network Protocols (Use Wireshark to capture network traffic, identify different

3. IP Addressing and Subnetting (Calculate subnet masks, create subnets, assign IP addresses, and
verify using subnetting tools.)
4. VLAN Configuration (Create multiple VLANs, assign ports to VLANs, configure trunk ports, and
verify VLAN communication.)
5. Configuring a Firewall (Set up a firewall, configure inbound and outbound rules, and test the
effectiveness of the rules using different traffic scenarios.)
6. VPN Setup (Configure VPN settings on routers or dedicated VPN devices, establish a connection,
and verify secure data transmission.)
7. Network Monitoring with SNMP (Configure SNMP on network devices, use a network
monitoring tool to collect data, and analyse the performance metrics.)
8. User and Group Management (Create and manage user accounts, assign users to groups, set
permissions, and test access control.)
9. Network Troubleshooting with Ping and Traceroute (Simulate network issues, use ping and
traceroute commands to identify problems, and document the troubleshooting steps.)
10. Using Network Diagnostic Tools (Use tools like Nmap, Netstat, and ipconfig/ifconfig to gather
network information and troubleshoot common issues.)
11. Cloud Network Configuration (Use a cloud platform (e.g., AWS, Azure) to create a virtual
network, configure subnets, and establish connectivity between virtual machines.)
12. IPv6 Configuration (Configure IPv6 addresses on network devices, set up dual-stack
environments, and test IPv6 connectivity.)
13. Network Automation with Scripting (Write scripts using Python or Bash to automate network
configuration, deploy the scripts on network devices, and verify the automated setup.)

Module I: Advanced Ideation and Problem Refinement
Moving beyond basic brainstorming to advanced frameworks (e.g., TRIZ, Lateral Thinking,
I Disney Method). Deep dive into user empathy mapping, persona development, and 5
constructing "How Might We" (HMW) statements. Transitioning from the Semester IV
generic problem-solving to a highly targeted, customer-centric problem definition.
Module II: Design Thinking & Human-Centered Design (HCD)
Principles of Human-Centered Design (HCD). Mapping the customer journey (Touchpoints,
II Pain points, Moments of Truth). Understanding ergonomics, usability, aesthetics, and 5
emotional design. Balancing desirability (what people want) with feasibility (what is
technically possible) and viability (what makes business sense).
Module III: Architecture of a Prototype – Hardware, Software & Services
Anatomy of a prototype. Low-fidelity vs. High-fidelity prototyping strategy.
• For Physical Products: Materials, 3D printing/rapid manufacturing concepts, form
factors.
III 5
• For Digital/Software Products: User Interface (UI) and User Experience (UX)
basics, wireframing, mockups, and no-code/low-code tools.
• For Service Products: Service blueprints, storyboarding, role-playing, and
customer experience workflows.
Module IV: The MVP Framework and Agile Development
The philosophy of the Minimum Viable Product (MVP). Differentiating between a
IV prototype, a smoke test, and an MVP. Defining the "Core Value Proposition" features vs. 5
"Nice-to-Have" features (Feature Prioritization Matrix like MoSCoW method). Introduction
to Agile development cycles, Scrum basics, and iterative sprint planning for rapid building.
Simulation, and User Validation
Designing validation experiments. Alpha and Beta testing frameworks. Setting up usability
testing metrics (Task completion rates, error rates, User Satisfaction scores). Collecting
V 5
qualitative feedback through structured user interviews and observation. Introduction to
digital/physical simulation tools to test structural or software integrity before physical
deployment. Module V: Product Testing,
Module VI: Iteration Dynamics and Design for Scalability
Analyzing user test data to make data-driven design decisions. The Pivot vs. Persevere
framework. Introduction to "Design for Excellence" (DFX) concepts: Design for
VI 5
Manufacturing (DFM), Design for Assembly (DFA), and cost optimization of the prototype.
Documenting the technical design (Bill of Materials, Schematics, or Software Architecture
charts) to hand off to Semester VI (Strategy) and Semester VII (Scaling).

List of Experiments / Lab Activities
Each project group works on one of six pre-defined Need Statements; split into three functional
sub-teams — Team A (Mechanics & Kinematics), Team B (Actuation & Embedded/Sensing) and

functionality at a defined Integration Gate. In addition, every group completes a common ROS 2
foundation track (workspace, packages, nodes, and simulation) and integrates ROS 2 as a data-
exchange and visualization layer over the project's runtime interface.
Group of 3 to 5 students per sub-team; each project theme (Need Statement) is shared by three sub-

• Clarity of the problem: understanding of the assigned Need Statement, and clarity of the sub-team's

• Innovativeness in solutions, including creative design/engineering choices made within the stated
constraints.
• Cost effectiveness and societal impact of the proposed solution.
• Compliance with agreed Interfaces (I1 — Configuration, I2 — Runtime) and completion of contract

• Effective use of skill sets relevant to the sub-team's role (mechanics / electronics / software) and

• Contribution of individuals as a member or coordinator within the sub-team.

defining objectives of the work, and the methodology to be adopted.
LA-I is based on the efforts by the student for synopsis preparation. It shall be evaluated using the parameters
extent of literature review, scope defined, objectives, fundamental concepts, quality of presentation, and
interaction during presentation, effort/work done, quality of report and interaction with guide.
LA-II is based on the progress made during the semester for the objectives defined in the synopsis and the
report submitted by the students. It shall be evaluated through progress seminar(s) at the end of the semester.
The parameters for evaluation include extent of work done, results and discussion/publication efforts, quality
of presentation, quality of report, interaction during presentation and interaction with guide.
ESE will have end semester presentation. End semester presentation will include the validation work and
completion of nearly half the work defined for the dissertation. The literature review should continue to

study the latest research material available in the chosen field. The external examiner should assess the work
done by the individual student based on the detailed report on identification of topic for the work, the
methodology adopted and presentation followed by viva-voce. The parameters for evaluation include results
and discussion/publication efforts, quality of presentation, quality of report and interaction during
presentation.

Module Contents
The dissertation work will start in semester III, and should involve scientific research, design, collection,
and analysis of data, determining solutions and must bring out the individual’s contribution. Dissertation
Phase 1 will have presentation and report submission. The presentation will include identification of the
research problem based on the extensive literature review on the topic referring to latest literature available,
defining objectives of the work, and the methodology to be adopted.
LA-I is based on the efforts by the student for synopsis preparation. It shall be evaluated using the
parameters extent of literature review, scope defined, objectives, fundamental concepts, quality of
presentation, and interaction during presentation, effort/work done, quality of report and interaction with
guide.
LAI shall be conducted by Departmental Post-Graduate Committee (DPGC)
LA-II is based on the progress made during the semester for the objectives defined in the synopsis and the
report submitted by the students. It shall be evaluated through progress seminar(s) at the end of the semester.

The parameters for evaluation include extent of work done, results and discussion/publication efforts,
quality of presentation, quality of report, interaction during presentation and interaction with guide.
LA II shall be conducted by Departmental Post-Graduate Committee (DPGC)
ESE will have end semester presentation. End semester presentation will include the validation work and
completion of nearly half the work defined for the dissertation. The literature review should continue to
study the latest research material available in the chosen field. The external examiner should assess the work
done by the individual student based on the detailed report on identification of topic for the work, the
methodology adopted and presentation followed by viva-voce. The parameters for evaluation include results
and discussion/publication efforts, quality of presentation, quality of report and interaction during
presentation.
ESE shall be conducted at the end of semester by a duly constituted examination panel composed of Chairman,
internal examiner (guide) and external examiner.

Module Module Contents Hours
I CAD Environment and Digital Design Infrastructure 6
Evolution and role of CAD in modern engineering design workflow; classification of CAD
systems from 2D drafting to parametric solid design; CAD workstation architecture and
hardware requirements; overview of commercial CAD software platforms; Product Data
Management (PDM) and Product Lifecycle Management (PLM); CAD data exchange
standards and interoperability (IGES, STEP, STL); cloud-based and collaborative CAD
platforms; Digital Twin concept and relevance to Industry 4.0; AI-assisted geometric
generation and intelligent design support tools.
II CAD Communication Networks and Data Exchange 6
Fundamentals of computer communication for CAD applications; network classification —
LAN, WAN, intranet, and internet-based engineering systems; principles of data
transmission and communication protocols; client-server architecture and distributed
engineering databases; network-enabled engineering workflows and concurrent engineering
concepts; remote engineering coordination and version management; engineering data
security, access control, and intellectual property considerations; enterprise-level
engineering information exchange & CAD connectivity with industrial information systems.
Course Contents for M. Tech Programme, Department of Mechanical Engineering, AY2026-27

III Geometric Transformations and CAD Graphics 6
Coordinate systems in CAD — Cartesian, cylindrical, and spherical systems; global and
local coordinate frames; geometric transformations in 2D and 3D — translation, scaling,
rotation, reflection, and shearing; homogeneous coordinate formulation; concatenated
transformations and transformation sequence dependency; geometric mapping and
coordinate system conversion; inverse transformations; windowing, viewing, and clipping
operations in CAD graphics systems.
IV Geometric Representation of Curves and Surfaces 7
Orthographic, isometric, axonometric, parallel, and perspective projections; parametric and
non-parametric curve formulations; analytic curves — lines, circles, and conics; synthetic
curves — Hermite spline, Bezier, B-Spline, and NURBS representations; geometric
continuity concepts (C0, C1, C2); curve editing operations — joining, splitting, and degree
elevation; parametric surface patches — Bezier, B-Spline, and NURBS surfaces; surface
operations — trimming, blending, and offsetting; computational implementation of curve
generation techniques in an interactive environment.
Solid Representation Techniques
V 7
Limitations of wireframe and surface representations; Boundary Representation (B-rep) —
topological entities, Euler’s law, winged-edge and half-edge data structures; Constructive
Solid Geometry (CSG) — primitives, Boolean operations, and CSG tree representation;
sweep-based solid generation — translational, rotational, and path-based sweeps;
comparison of B-rep and CSG techniques; feature-based representation and manufacturing-
oriented features; parametric and variational design approaches — constraint-based
geometry creation and preservation of engineering intent.
VI Advanced Solid Representation and CAD Applications 7
Analytic Solid Modelling (ASM); alternative solid representation schemes — cell
decomposition, spatial occupancy enumeration, and octree methods; local solid editing
operations and manipulation techniques; mass property evaluation of solid models;
mechanical tolerancing and tolerance stack-up analysis; reverse engineering and surface
reconstruction from point cloud data; meshing methods for engineering analysis — FEM
meshing, mesh quality assessment, and mesh generation techniques; generative design and
constraint-driven automated design alternatives; lattice structures for lightweight
engineering applications; AI applications in CAD — intelligent assistance, knowledge-
driven engineering, and computational design automation.

Credits: 12
Course Objectives
To develop the student to apply the knowledge gained to identify problems for research and
1
provide the solutions by self-study and interaction with stakeholders.
2 Acquire knowledge to tackle real world problems of societal concerns
3 Impart flexibility to the student to have increased control over his/ her learning
4 Enhance a students’ learning through increased interaction with peers and colleagues.
Course Outcomes (CO) with Bloom’s Taxonomy Level
At the end of the course, the students will be able to,
Bloom’s Bloom’s
CO Course Outcome Statement/s Taxonomy Taxonomy
Level Description

III Applying
problems in the project.

identifying patterns, trends, and potential areas for improvement.
CO3 Evaluate the effectiveness of different approaches and techniques
employed in their project, and propose modifications or V Evaluating
enhancements as necessary.
CO4 Design and develop innovative solutions, products, or systems that
address specific challenges or opportunities within their field of VI Creating
study.
List of Experiments / Lab Activities/Topics
The third semester is completely devoted to dissertation work
which is defined based on the interest of the students to specialize in a particular area.
Student is expected to carry out independent research work on the chosen topic. In this semester
it is expected that the student has carried out substantial research work including exhaustive
literature survey, formulation of the research problem, development/fabrication of experimental
set-up (if any/required) and testing, and analysis of initial results thus obtained. In fourth
semester, the student continues his/her dissertation work. It is expected that the student has
completed most of the experimental/computation works and analysed the results so obtained as
proposed in the synopsis. The work should be completed in all respects in this semester. The
student is required to submit the dissertation work in the form of report as per the institute rule.

Course Objectives
To familiarize a student with the basics of electrical engineering that are essential for better
1 understanding on how to integrate Renewable energy sources and operate and model the power
network.
2 To make students familiar with the basics of most clean and renewable energy technologies
To understand the concepts of solar cells, underlying physics, optoelectronic processes and
3
techniques used for photovoltaic characterization.
Course Outcomes (CO) with Bloom’s Taxonomy Level
At the end of the course, the students will be able to,
Bloom’s Bloom’s
CO Course Outcome Statement/s Taxonomy Taxonomy
Level Description
CO1 Interpret thermal conversion and storage routes for solar energy III Applying
CO2 Interpret the photovoltaic devices and their fundamentals III Applying
CO3 Analyze the environmental and social impact of various generation
IV Analyzing
technologies
CO4 Analyze recent technological advancements in sustainable power
generation and assess their potential to improve efficiency, reduce IV Analyzing
costs, and enhance sustainability
Module Module Contents Hours
Introduction to power generation
I Global and Indian scenario, an overview of current technologies available for 4
power generation, Concept of the renewable energy- based power plant
Solar Thermal Power Generation
Fundamentals of Solar thermal energy conversion, solar thermal based power
plant design and analysis (flat plate and concentrator), ORC, RC, and Stirling
engine.
II 7
Solar Photovoltaic Power Generation
Fundamentals of Solar photovoltaic energy conversion, Solar PV power plant
design, Performance analysis of standalone and grid connected PV systems.

Wind Power Generation
Introduction to wind turbine, classification and analysis of different
components, Theory, design and analysis of wind turbines (horizontal axis and
vertical axis) and wind farms.
III 7
Hydro Power Generation
Introduction to hydro power plant, overview of micro, mini and small hydro
power plants, hydraulic turbines, Selection and design criteria of pumps and
turbines, Brief theory, design and analysis of hydro power plants
Biomass Power Generation
Fundamentals of bioenergy production technologies through different routes,
design and analysis of biochemical and thermochemical reactors for clean
power generation and value- added products, IGCC.
IV 7
Hydrogen energy and fuel cells
Importance, various routes of hydrogen generation, basic principle and design
of different types of fuel cells and their applications, future prospects, IGFC
Geothermal Energy
Fundamentals, classification, theory, design and analysis of geothermal power
plant
Ocean Thermal Energy
V Fundamentals, classification, theory, design and analysis of ocean thermal 7
power plant
Wave and Tidal Energy
Fundamentals, classification, theory, design, and analysis of wave and tidal
power plant
Energy Storage
Different modes of energy storage; design and analysis of different
technologies for thermal, mechanical, and electro-chemical energy storage
systems
VI 7
Energy Economics
Cost analysis, interest, Accounting rate of return, Payback, Discounted cash
flow, Net present value, Internal rate of return, Inflation and life cycle analysis
of energy systems.

List of Experiments / Lab Activities/Topics
Contents:
The Mini Project and Seminar shall commence in Semester-II and should preferably address a problem of
significant research relevance in the field of Electronics and Communication Engineering. The work shall
involve the identification and formulation of a research problem, comprehensive review of scientific and
technical literature, design and development of suitable methodologies, generation or collection of data,
analysis and interpretation of results, and formulation of an effective solution. The mini project is expected
to encourage originality, innovation, and independent thinking, while highlighting the individual
contribution of the student.
The seminar shall preferably be based on the area in which the student intends to undertake the dissertation
work. Students shall identify and investigate contemporary engineering challenges and emerging research
domains through an extensive literature survey and critical review of research publications, journals,
conference proceedings, patents, and technical reports. The study may focus on recent advances in areas
such as advanced communication systems, Internet of Things (IoT), embedded systems, VLSI design, signal
and image processing, artificial intelligence, machine learning, wireless communications, and other related
technologies.
Course Contents for M. Tech. Programme in Electronics and Communication Engineering,
Department of Electronics Engineering, AY 2026-27

Each student shall undertake a Mini Project involving problem formulation, system design, modeling,
simulation, implementation, testing, validation, and performance evaluation using appropriate engineering
tools, techniques, and methodologies. The seminar presentation shall be based on the Mini Project
undertaken and should demonstrate a clear understanding of the problem, methodology adopted, results
obtained, and critical analysis of the findings. The presentation should also highlight the effectiveness and
limitations of the proposed solution and indicate possible directions for future work. The course shall
emphasize technical report writing, effective presentation skills, research ethics, plagiarism awareness,
intellectual property rights, and professional communication practices. These activities are intended to
prepare students for advanced research, innovation, and lifelong learning in the field of Electronics and
Communication Engineering.
Students shall maintain regular interaction with their project guide, and the topic of the Mini Project and
Seminar shall be selected through mutual consultation between the student and the guide. Evaluation shall
be based on the quality of the work carried out, periodic progress, seminar presentation, and the final report.
The report shall include the literature review, detailed problem statement, methodology, design and
implementation aspects, experimental or simulation results, analysis and discussion, case studies (where
applicable), conclusions, and references. The completed work shall be presented before a panel of examiners
constituted by the Department Postgraduate Committee for assessment and evaluation.

List of Experiments / Lab Activities/Topics
List of Lab Activities:
Students are expected to undertake independent research work on their chosen topic. During this
semester, the following tasks should be accomplished:
1. Independent Research Work:
o Initiate and conduct independent research on the chosen topic.
2. Literature Survey:
o Perform an exhaustive literature survey to gain a comprehensive understanding of
existing work and identify gaps.
3. Research Problem Formulation:
o Formulate a clear and well-defined research problem based on the literature survey.
4. Experimental Setup Development/Fabrication (if applicable):
o Develop or fabricate the necessary experimental setup required for the research. This
may include hardware, software, or computational tools.
5. Initial Testing and Analysis:
o Conduct initial testing using the developed experimental setup.
o Analyze the preliminary results obtained from the initial tests.
6. Documentation:
o Document all research activities, including literature survey findings, problem
formulation, experimental setup, and initial results analysis.

Lab activities for Dissertation Phase-I shall encompass a range of research-focused tasks, tailored to
support independent research work. These activities may include but are not limited to:
1. Experiments:

o Performing 8-10 carefully planned experiments to gather initial data.
2. Mini-Projects:
o Working on mini-projects that contribute to the larger dissertation goal.

 Literature reviews and documentation

Module 1: Introduction and Overview
In Module 1, students will gain an understanding of co-curricular and extracurricular
activities, distinguishing between the two and recognizing their significance in personal and
professional development. The module will introduce the course objectives, emphasizing the
expected outcomes and how they will be assessed throughout the program.
Module 2: Leadership and Teamwork Skills
Module 2 focuses on developing leadership and teamwork abilities essential for effective
collaboration. Students will explore various leadership styles and theories, learn practical
skills such as delegation, decision-making, and problem-solving. They will also delve into the
dynamics of teamwork, understanding roles within teams, and techniques for managing
conflicts. Practical exercises and team projects will reinforce these concepts.
Module 3: Communication Skills
Module 3 centers on enhancing communication skills crucial for effective interaction in
professional settings. Students will refine both verbal and non-verbal communication
techniques, practice public speaking and presentation skills, and hone their writing proficiency
in professional and technical contexts, including emails and reports.
Module 4: Time Management and Organizational Skills
Module 4 addresses the importance of time management and organizational skills in balancing
academic, co-curricular, and extracurricular activities. Students will learn principles of
effective time management, develop strategies for setting priorities and goals, create and
maintain schedules, and utilize tools to enhance productivity and organization.
Module 5: Social Responsibility and Community Engagement
Module 5 emphasizes social responsibility and community engagement. Students will explore
the concept of social responsibility, understand its significance in contributing to society, and
engage in community service projects aimed at addressing local needs. They will also learn to
advocate for social causes through awareness campaigns and utilize platforms like social
media for social good.
Module 6: Professional Development and Networking
Module 6 focuses on professional development and networking. Students will be introduced
to various professional organizations relevant to their field of study, exploring the benefits of
membership and opportunities for career growth. They will develop networking skills, build
and maintain professional relationships, participate in networking events, and engage in
activities that support lifelong learning and career advancement. Additionally, the module will
cover self-assessment techniques, reflective practices for personal growth, and the importance
of peer feedback and mentorship in professional development.

Following activities are to be carried out in dissertation:

dissertation work.

challenges and expected outcomes

references, nearly absolute contents. Use of plagiarism tools.

software engineering practices

and other dependency documents. Preferable use online code repositories (github/bitbucket)
The students are required to submit the dissertation work in the form of report as per the institute rule.

soft copy on CD/DVD (with code, PPT, PDF, Text report document & reference material) or on an online
repository.

Course Description:
Managerial Economics applies economic concepts and analytical tools to real-world business decision-
making. The course helps MBA students understand how demand, costs, pricing, competition, market
conditions, macroeconomic conditions and economic policies influence managerial decisions.
The course focuses on developing economic reasoning, analytical thinking, and decision-making skills.
Students will learn to apply concepts such as demand and supply, elasticity, production and cost
analysis, market structures, pricing strategies, profit maximization, and risk and uncertainty to practical
business situations.
Through cases, numerical exercises, discussions, and current business examples, the course connects
economic theory with managerial practice and enables students to make informed and strategic business
decisions.
Pre-requisites (prior conditions to register for the course, if any):
NA
Course Learning Outcomes:
After completing this course, the participants should be able to:
 CLO1: Explain key economic concepts and their relevance to managerial decision-making.
 CLO2: Analyze demand, supply, elasticity, and consumer behaviour to support business
decisions.
 CLO3: Apply production, cost, revenue, and profit concepts to solve managerial problems.
 CLO4: Assess the impact of macroeconomic factors such as inflation, interest rates,
economic growth, and government policies on business decisions.
 CLO5: Apply economic analysis to real-world business situations and recommend
appropriate managerial strategies.
Pedagogy:

The course will use a practical, application-oriented pedagogy combining:
 Interactive Lectures & Presentations – Concepts explained through business examples.
 Case Studies – Application of economic concepts to real-world business situations.
 Class Discussions & Debates – Critical thinking on current economic and business issues.
 Numerical & Problem-Solving Exercises – Application of demand, cost, pricing, and profit
concepts.
 Current Business & Economic Events – Connecting classroom concepts with market
developments.
 Group Projects & Presentations – Collaborative analysis of real-world business problems.

MS-Excel, MS-PowerPoint

Course Description:
Accounting for Managers equips students with the knowledge and skills to understand, interpret and use
accounting information for managerial decision-making. The course covers financial statements,
financial analysis, cost management, budgeting, CVP analysis and performance evaluation, with
emphasis on practical business applications and case-based learning.
The course is designed to help students from diverse academic backgrounds connect accounting concepts
with planning, control, profitability, resource allocation and strategic decision-making
Pre-requisites:
NA
Course Learning Outcomes:
After completion of this course, students will be able to:
CLO1: Explain2 key financial and management accounting concepts, principles and their role in
managerial planning and decision-making.
CLO2: Prepare3 and Interpret4 financial statements to assess the financial position and
performance of a business.
CLO3: Analyze4 financial and operational performance using ratio analysis, comparative
analysis, cost analysis and relevant performance measures.
CLO4: Apply3 costing, budgeting and cost-volume-profit techniques to support planning, control
and resource allocation decisions.
CLO5: Evaluate5 accounting information and managerial alternatives to make informed short-
term and strategic business decisions
Pedagogy:
The course will use a practical, application-oriented pedagogy combining:

 Concept-based lectures for accounting fundamentals.
 Numerical exercises for developing analytical skills.
 Case studies based on real business situations.
 Annual report analysis of Indian companies.
 Class discussions and problem-solving for managerial decision-making.
 Group activities and presentations to develop interpretation and communication skills.
 Excel-based exercises for financial and cost analysis

Course Description:
Marketing Management is a foundational course that develops an understanding of how organizations
analyze markets, understand customer needs, create and deliver customer value, and build sustainable
competitive advantage. It covers the role of marketing in business, marketing environment, consumer
behavior, market segmentation, targeting, positioning, and value proposition development.
The course further examines key marketing decisions related to products and brands, innovation, pricing,
distribution and channels, and integrated marketing communications. It also introduces contemporary
areas such as digital and social media marketing, omnichannel marketing, AI-enabled marketing, and
marketing performance measurement, providing students with an integrated foundation for analyzing
marketing problems and formulating effective marketing strategies.
Pre-requisites:
Basic familiarity with business, economics and quantitative reasoning is helpful.
Course Learning Outcomes:
After completion of this course, students will be able to:
CLO1: Explain2 core marketing concepts, the marketing orientation, customer value
creation, marketing planning and the role of marketing in business strategy.
CLO2: Analyze4 consumer and market information to segment markets, select target customers, and
formulate differentiated positioning and value propositions.
CLO3: Evaluate5 product, brand, pricing and channel decisions using appropriate managerial
frameworks and quantitative/qualitative evidence
CLO4: Design6 integrated marketing communication and digital engagement strategies that connect
customer journeys, channels, content and measurable outcomes.
CLO5: Develop6 and defend an integrated marketing plan for a real business problem, including
objectives, STP, positioning, 4Ps, implementation priorities and performance metrics
Pedagogy:

Each module comprises six sessions: The first two focus on core theoretical concepts (L); the next
two use engaging and interactive teaching to deepen and apply concepts (I); and the final two are
dedicated to an anchor business case and its practical application (I).
• Core concept lectures for foundational frameworks and terminology.
• Interactive lectures using questioning, discussion, examples, short problem-solving, role plays,
debates, brand audits and decision exercises.
• Two dedicated case-discussion sessions in every module, with one anchor case per module.
• Two industry-expert sessions focused on live marketing practice, tools, decisions and employer
expectations.
• Continuous assessment through assignments, submissions, case analysis, presentations, role plays
and other classroom activities.
• An integrated marketing application project culminating in a managerial recommendation and
presentation.
Software/other requirements (if any):
MS Excel/Google Sheets, MS PowerPoint/Canva, access to web and digital advertising/social
platforms for observation.

Course Description:
Human Resource Management introduces the core processes through which organizations attract,
develop, motivate, and retain the people who create competitive advantage - approached simultaneously
through an academic lens (the frameworks and evidence base of the discipline) and an industry lens
(what a practicing HR generalist or line manager is actually expected to do). The course moves from
strategic HR and workforce planning, through recruitment, selection, training, and performance
management, to compensation design, employee relations, culture, and HR analytics, treating HR not
as an administrative support function but as a lever for organizational performance.
The course is built around six real, extensively-taught business cases - one per module - supplemented
by numerical and design exercises, two practitioner-led sessions, and a capstone HR-strategy project,
so that students finish the course having designed, analyzed and defended actual HR artefacts (a job
description, a compensation structure, a performance system, an HR strategy) rather than only having
studied the subject.
The course is equally relevant to students planning HR careers and to those entering general
management, consulting, or entrepreneurial roles were managing people well is a core determinant of
success.
Pre-requisites (prior conditions to register for the course, if any):
NA
Course Learning Outcomes:
After completing this course, the participants should be able to:
CLO1: Explain² the strategic role of HRM, the HR value chain, and how people practices create
sustainable competitive advantage.
CLO2: Design⁶ a job analysis, workforce plan, and a valid, bias-aware recruitment and selection
process, including the use of AI-based screening tools.

CLO3: Evaluate⁵ training, development and performance management interventions using
evidence-based HR frameworks (ADDIE, OKRs/MBO, 360-degree feedback).
CLO4: Design⁶ compensation structures and incentive systems that balance internal equity,
external competitiveness, statutory compliance and motivation.
CLO5: Diagnose⁴ employee engagement, culture and industrial-relations issues, and propose
interventions grounded in current Indian labour law and organisational-behaviour
evidence.
CLO6: Develop⁶ and defend an integrated HR strategy for a real organisation, using people
analytics to justify recommendations.
Pedagogy:
The course uses a case-method and application-oriented pedagogy. Sessions will be
conducted/supplemented by:
 Conceptual mini-lectures followed by design exercises rather than long theory-only sessions.
 Six anchor cases (one per module) - Southwest Airlines, GROW (AI-based recruitment),
Google’s Project Oxygen, Lincoln Electric, HCL Technologies, and Netflix - with pre-read
preparation, cold calls, team analysis and decision recommendations.
 Numerical and design exercises: job evaluation, pay-structure design, incentive calculations,
workforce-planning forecasts and HR metrics.
 Role-plays and simulations: a structured selection interview, a performance-appraisal
conversation, and a grievance-handling negotiation.
 Two substantially practitioner-led industry sessions connected directly to course concepts
(performance management/people analytics, and employee relations/culture).
 A group capstone project in which students design and defend an end-to-end HR strategy for a
real or chosen organization.
 Selective use of contemporary Indian examples (labour codes, gig-economy platforms, IT-
sector HR practices) to connect frameworks to current practice.
Software/other requirements (if any):
MS Excel/Google Sheets (compensation and people-analytics exercises), MS PowerPoint/Canva, a
free-tier HRIS/people-analytics dashboard demo, access to job portals (LinkedIn, Naukri) for a live job-
posting/sourcing exercise.

Module 1: Foundations of HRM & Strategic Human Resource Management
Learning Objectives:
1. Explain the strategic role of HRM and the evolution from personnel administration to a strategic HR partner.
2. Analyse the environmental context of HRM in India (labour market, demographics, gig economy, statutory

Application / Capstone Project Component:
Project / problem statement: In groups of 4–5, students select a real organisation (their own
workplace/internship, a family business, or a company they can access via secondary research and 1–
2 practitioner interviews) and design an integrated HR strategy covering: (a) a workforce plan and one
full recruitment & selection process for a real/realistic role, (b) a performance-management design for
that role/team, (c) a compensation and incentive structure benchmarked against comparable roles, and
(d) an employee-engagement and culture diagnosis with at least one concrete intervention.
Individual or Group Group (4–5 students); the final viva includes individual questioning to assess each
member's contribution and understanding.

Expected Student Output A written HR-strategy report (12–15 pages) plus a 15-minute group presentation and
defence (viva), covering workforce planning, recruitment & selection design, performance
management, compensation design, and an engagement/culture intervention for the chosen
organisation.
Evaluation Criteria Diagnostic quality and use of real data/evidence; internal consistency of the HR strategy
across sub-components; rigor of the compensation/incentive design; feasibility and
specificity of the engagement intervention; quality of the presentation and individual viva
performance.
Timeline Organisation & problem selection by Session 8; interim workforce plan + recruitment
design due at Session 18; full report and presentation at Session 30.

Course Description:
Business Productivity Tools is a fully practical course that develops the digital fluency expected of an
MBA graduate for analysing information, communicating professionally, managing work, using artificial
intelligence responsibly, automating repetitive processes, and presenting data-driven insights. The course
covers spreadsheets and data tools, professional communication and presentation tools, generative AI
assistants and AI-assisted coding, task and project management platforms, workflow automation, and
business intelligence using Microsoft Power BI.
The course is designed as a transferable productivity toolkit for the rest of the MBA programme. Students
repeatedly work with realistic business situations—such as sales reporting, budgeting, marketing
analysis, project tracking, research, meeting follow-ups, workflow automation and management
dashboards—and produce working outputs rather than only learning software features. Tool selection is
taught from a managerial perspective: students learn what to use, when to use it, how to combine tools,
how to verify outputs, and how to communicate the resulting business insight.
Pre-requisites:
1. Basic computer literacy and familiarity with operating a computer, managing files and folders,
and using a web browser.
2. Basic familiarity with spreadsheets and common office applications is desirable but not
mandatory.
3. Students should have access to a personal laptop capable of running the required web-based and
desktop productivity tools.
4. No prior programming, data analytics, or AI experience is required; the course introduces these
capabilities progressively.
Course Learning Outcomes:
After completion of this course, students will be able to:
CLO1: Apply³ spreadsheet and data tools to structure, clean, analyse and model business data and produce
decision-useful summaries and dashboards.
CLO2: Create⁶ professional business communication and presentation artefacts using email,
collaborative workspaces and presentation/design tools.

CLO3: Apply³ generative AI, prompt-engineering and AI-assisted coding tools to business tasks while
verifying outputs and following responsible-use practices.
CLO4: Build⁶ practical task and project-management workflows using Notion and Trello to plan, assign,
track and review work.
CLO5: Design⁶, test and troubleshoot no-code/low-code workflows using Zapier, Make and Power
Automate to automate recurring business processes
CLO6: Develop⁶ interactive Power BI reports and dashboards by connecting, modelling and visualising
business data to communicate actionable insights
Pedagogy:
 All 56 sessions are conducted in a computer laboratory. The default pattern is a short
concept/demo (approximately 10–15 minutes) followed by guided build-along practice, individual
application and a short output check.
 Students work with realistic business datasets, emails, documents, project briefs and workflow
problems. The emphasis is on transfer: the same skill should be usable in Marketing, Accounting,
Finance, HR, Operations, Research Methods and other MBA courses.
 Every module ends with an applied challenge/deliverable that contributes to ISE. Students are
expected to save and submit working files, not screenshots alone.
 AI tools are taught as assistants rather than authorities. Verification, source checking, privacy,
confidentiality, hallucination/error detection and human review are embedded in the exercises.
 Tool exposure is broad, but depth is prioritised on the capabilities most useful to an MBA
graduate. Students are not expected to become software specialists; they are expected to become
competent business users who can select, combine and supervise digital tools

click sequence; they must understand the business requirement and choose an appropriate
workflow.

Course Description:
Corporate Readiness Program I equips first-year MBA students with the career, professional, analytical,
and industry-readiness skills required to succeed in the summer internship process and beyond. Unlike
the other Term 1 courses, this is a skill-and-practicum course built around five domains: career foundation
and personal branding, professional communication, analytical/quantitative skills, sector and career
awareness, and integrated placement readiness.
The course is deliberately practitioner-heavy: a personalised 1:1 career-coaching session, six industry-
sector workshops, and a panel-evaluated mock interview mean every student engages directly with
practitioners multiple times across the term, not just twice. Every session ends with the student producing
or performing something - a roadmap, a resume, a mock GD performance, a dashboard, a mock interview
- rather than only studying the subject.
By the end of the course, every student should be able to walk into the placement process with a complete,
tested professional toolkit: a role-aligned resume, an optimised LinkedIn profile, practiced
GD/presentation/interview performance, working quantitative and Excel skills, and an informed view of
which industry sectors and roles fit them best..

Pedagogy:
This is an experiential, practicum-first course. Sessions are conducted/supplemented by:
● Interactive workshops for career development, communication, personal branding, and analytical
skills.
● 1:1 career coaching through a personalised domain-expert interaction (Session 2).
● Applied practice: resume building, GDs, presentations, aptitude, logical reasoning, Excel and data
visualisation exercises, each ending in a produced/performed output.
● Industry exposure through six sector-specific workshops led by practitioners from each sector.
● Simulations and mock assessments: two rounds of mock GD and two rounds of mock interviews,
each with individual, recorded feedback.
● A progressively-built Career Readiness Portfolio (roadmap, resume, LinkedIn, sector-fit note,
interview reflection) that is scoped early and finalised as the course capstone

TCC Saarthi platform (resume builder, aptitude/GD/interview question banks, AI-based
evaluation where applicable, progress tracking); MS Excel; MS PowerPoint/Canva; a
student-owned LinkedIn account; a recording setup (Zoom recording or equivalent) for mock
GD/interview playback and feedback.

Credit System and Bank 2025-26
Credit System and Bank
The WCE curriculum is structured across multiple academic years, each year consisting of two semesters, and includes a mix of mandatory and elective courses. Apart from classroom expert lectures, experiential learning is enabled through hands-on sessions in Labs, field work,  project works and internships. Each course is assigned credits, as a measure of learning effort expected to be invested by students.

Typically, one credit is assigned for one hour of instruction per week through lectures or tutorials. For laboratory sessions, mini-projects, or seminars, one credit is awarded for every two hours of student engagement per week. For undergraduate students admitted in the academic year 2023-24 and beyond, 174 credits must be earned to obtain a Bachelor’s degree in an Engineering discipline with a Multi-Disciplinary Minor. Whereas for earning a Masters one need to earn 80 credits in the span of minimum four semesters.

WCE follows a choice-based credit system, offering partial flexibility within its autonomous academic programs. Students can select courses from a range of Open Electives, Multi-Disciplinary streams, and Program Electives. Students may select the best courses or combination of courses to suit their aptitude and quest for knowledge.

Additionally, WCE is part of the Academic Bank of Credit (ABC) system, launched by the Government of India. As a result, these credits are digitally recorded in unique student accounts, which are recognized nationwide. All academic credits earned through WCE, partnering institutes and online approved platforms are stored, acknowledged, maintained, accumulated, transferred, validated, and can be redeemed for the purpose of degree certification.

ill) Reducing frequency of alumni meet.

placement reaching 79%, the members noticed low placement in the Civil engineering batch.
The Director suggested that the local civil contractors should be invited to interact with
students for securing job offers, especially for graduating civil engineers. The Director also
wanted to know what vocations the remaining students pursue. The IQAC Coordinator
assured Director about acting on the suggestions in the current semester. The members also
expressed satisfaction over the progress of TEQIP during this period. Resolved that the
activity report is noted.

Engineering Department for deputation as State Project Adviser (SPA) at DTE
Rajasthan
The IQAC Coordinator informed the Council that Dr. U. A. Dabade has been selected as
State Project Adviser at the Directorate of Technical Education, Jaipur, for supervising
implementation of TEQIP in Rajasthan State. He has applied for the Council’s permission to
join as SPA in Jaipur on deputation till the end of TEQIP phase III, i.e. September 2020. The
members desired to know about faculty position in Mechanical Engineering dept. and
whether arrangements have been made for academic workload in case Dr. Dabade’s request
for deputation is permitted. The IQAC Coordinator assured the members about proper
arrangements being made for completion of students’ course work. It was then

Project Adviser for a period till end of TEQIP phase III is approved.
Item No. 4. To consider allowing Associate Professors and Assistant Professors with
PhD
For various administrative positions in the institute the IQAC Coordinator explained that at
present, we consider only professors for assigning responsibilities like Dean and Head of
Department. Since there are total of only 8 professors across all departments, we are presently
giving these responsibilities to senior Associate Professors as In-Charge. This is not
appreciated by visiting committees of NBA, NAAC, UGC, etc. The IQAC Coordinator,
therefore, tabled a proposal to allow other faculty members who are associate/assistant
professors with Ph. D. qualifications to be considered for giving the responsibilities of
department Head and Deans. He informed the members that such practice is followed in other
institutes and even at IlTs.
The members discussed the proposal and considered that allowing assistant and associate
professors also to share these responsibilities should improve faculty participation in college
administration. After discussions, it was then Resolved that the proposal to consider associate
professors and assistant professors with Ph. D. qualifications is approved in principle and the
In-Charge Director is asked to frame guidelines for allocating duties of Deans and HODs
from among eligible faculty members.
